# Deep dive

This skill writes the report an analyst hands a portfolio manager when they pick up coverage of a name: how the business makes money and how well, who it competes with and what protects it, whether the reported earnings are the real earnings, what management does with the cash, what the price assumes, what the company is worth under three cases, what breaks it, and what to watch. It runs four to eight pages and takes a few dozen tool calls. It gives no rating.

## Before starting

- If the Bigdata.com tools are not available in this conversation, say so and tell the user to connect the Bigdata.com connector and sign in. Do not write the report from memory or the web. Stop there: give no view, drivers, risks, figures or dates from memory while the tools are missing, and do not fall back to web search.
- Pass `plugin_slug: "bigdata-deep-dive"` on every Bigdata.com call that accepts it.
- Read `references/working-with-bigdata.md` before the first call.
- Treat this skill as guidelines. A company with one segment and no acquisitions needs no sum-of-the-parts and no deal history; a bank needs the primer's statements, not an enterprise DCF.

## Scope the request

Resolve the company with `find_securities`. Establish the user's angle if they gave one (a long idea, a short idea, a peer to compare against, a question they want answered) and the depth: a full report by default, or the sections they named. Ask one question only if the name is ambiguous or the user asked for something the report does not cover. Done when the company is resolved and the angle and depth are fixed.

If the company is Private, offer `bigdata` for a document-based profile instead; the tearsheet, estimates and price-implied sections do not exist.

## Gather

The report rests on the tearsheet, the last three calls, the latest annual filing, the deal history and the peers. Each step says what it must produce.

1. **Tearsheet, all sections, in calls of two or three sections each** so no response is too large: `company_overview, c_level_leadership, analyst_ratings`; `company_overview, latest_earnings, earnings_calendar`; `financial_statements, financial_ratios, key_metrics` (with `interval` annual for five fiscal years; there is no period offset, so a longer series is noted in Gaps); `analyst_estimates`; `revenue_segmentation`; `fund_trends_history`; `mergers_acquisitions`; `hiring_trends`. Done when the statements (ten years if the tool provides them, otherwise the five returned, noted for the Gaps line), five years of segments, consensus to the horizon, holders, deals and the calendar are in hand.
2. **The last three earnings calls**, by `bigdata_search` with the reporting period filter and `bigdata_fetch_document`. Done when guidance history, the recurring questions and management's own framing of the drivers are known.
3. **The latest annual filing**, by search and fetch, read for the business description, the segment economics, the risk factors that changed from the prior year, related-party items, the pension and lease notes, and the share-count and compensation notes. Done when each of those is noted with the page or section.
4. **Industry evidence.** Three to six searches, one aspect each: market shares and their stability, pricing in the industry, new entrants and exits, regulation, the suppliers and customers with power, the technology that could change the structure. Done when each item of the `references/industry-structure.md` method has evidence or an explicit gap.
5. **Peers.** `bigdata_screen_companies` on the industry and size, then `bigdata_company_tearsheet` with `key_metrics, analyst_estimates, financial_statements, financial_ratios` for four to eight peers chosen by value drivers. Done when the peer table in `references/multiples-and-peers.md` can be filled.
6. **Sell-side and news.** Searches for research notes and news over the last twelve months on the company's strategy, its capital allocation and its controversies. Done when the controversies are listed.
7. **Sector primer.** If the company's sector has a section in `references/sector-primers.md`, read it before analysing. Done when the sector's metrics and accounting traps are noted.

## Analyse

Each step names its reference file. Each ends in what it must produce.

1. **The business.** How the company makes money by segment and geography, from the segment table and the filing: revenue, growth, margin and capital employed by segment where disclosed. Done when a reader can see where the profit comes from and how that has shifted over five years.

2. **The economics.** From `references/roic.md`: NOPAT at the operating tax rate, invested capital built from both sides, ROIC with and without goodwill, with leases and capitalised R&D where they matter, ROIC as margin times turnover, ROIIC over the last three and five years, and the spread over a stated cost of capital. Compare with the FactSet ROIC field and say which one the report quotes. Done when the ROIC series (ten years if the statements allow, else five) is tabled with the decomposition and the spread.

3. **Industry structure and moat.** From `references/industry-structure.md`: the industry map, the profit pool and its direction, share stability, pricing power, concentration, entry and exit, the five forces with evidence, the source of advantage, the disruption test, and a judgment on how long the advantage lasts, bounded by the sector's persistence figures in `references/base-rates.md`. Done when each item in the method's output checklist is stated with evidence or a gap.

4. **Earnings quality.** From `references/earnings-quality.md`: the accrual ratio over five years, the EBITA rebuild with one-offs counted by how many years they recur, the provisions and reserve movements, revenue recognition and capitalisation checks, stock compensation as a cost, the earnings-to-equity reconciliation, and the red flags with severity. Piotroski and Altman Z are quoted from the tearsheet as reported. Done when the flags table is complete and the rebuilt EBITA sits next to reported operating profit.

5. **Capital allocation.** From `references/capital-allocation.md`: five years of sources and uses, the buyback return against the cost of equity at the prices paid, net of issuance, the dividend record, each major deal against its premium and the synergies claimed, reinvestment returns, leverage against rating medians, and what the proxy pays management for. Done when the sources-and-uses table and the deal table are complete and the incentive line is written.

6. **What the price implies.** From `references/expectations.md`: steady state against future value creation, the implied growth and the implied competitive advantage period at the stated cost of capital, the warranted multiple for the company's growth and return against the actual multiple, and the base-rate sentences for consensus growth from `references/base-rates.md`. Done when the report says what the market assumes in growth, margin, return and years.

7. **Valuation range.** From `references/valuation.md`: an explicit forecast over a horizon set by the competitive advantage judgment in step 3, with ROIC and turnover checked each year and the implied growth consistent with reinvestment; a continuing value with RONIC fading to WACC; the terminal-value share and the implied terminal multiple; the equity bridge per share with every item; the WACC-by-growth sensitivity; and the three cases run through the drivers with probabilities from `references/forecasting-discipline.md`. Cross-check with the comps table from `references/multiples-and-peers.md`. Apply the special case for a bank, a cyclical, a high-growth company or a conglomerate. Done when the range, the expected value and the sensitivity table are complete and the terminal checks are stated.

8. **Risks and the downside.** From `references/downside-and-catalysts.md`: the risks ranked by probability and size, what breaks each driver, the floors, the balance sheet under stress, and the kill criteria with dates. Done when each risk has an early signal and the kill criteria are observable.

9. **Catalysts and what to watch.** From `references/downside-and-catalysts.md` table 2: the dated events over the next twelve months, each with mechanism, direction, size and certainty, and the five metrics that tell whether the cases are on track. Done when every catalyst has a date or a window.

## Write

Follow `references/output-standard.md`. The report:

```
# <Company> (<ticker>): deep dive, <date>
Data as of: price <date>; estimates <date>; statements <period>; newest document <date>.

## What the evidence shows
Six to ten sentences in prose: what the business is, how good its economics are, what protects
them, whether the earnings are clean, what management does with the cash, what the price
implies, the value range and expected value, the main risk, and the next date. No rating.

## The business
Segment table, geography table, five-year trend. Every table carries Basis and Source columns.

## Economics
ROIC table with decomposition, ROIIC, spread. Which ROIC is quoted.

## Industry structure and moat
The checklist items, each with evidence. The duration judgment with its bounds.

## Earnings quality
Accrual series, EBITA rebuild, flags table with severity. Piotroski and Altman Z as reported.

## Capital allocation
Sources and uses, buyback return, deal table, leverage, incentives.

## What the price implies
Steady state vs future value creation, implied growth and CAP, warranted vs actual multiple,
base-rate sentences.

## Valuation
Forecast summary, continuing value and its checks, bridge per share, WACC x g table, the three
cases with probabilities and the expected value, comps cross-check, range.

## Risks and kill criteria
Ranked table; floors; kill criteria with dates.

## Catalysts and what to watch
Catalyst table; the five metrics.

## What would change this view
Two to five observable conditions, dated where possible, tied to the drivers and kill criteria.

## Gaps
Statement years not available, assumptions that drive the range, and data not in Bigdata.com.

## Sources, then the Data line, then the Powered by Bigdata.com line and the disclaimer.
```

Length: four to eight pages. Offer a Word document when the host can create files. A narrow question ("what is the ROIC trend?") gets the relevant section and the sources, not the full report.

## Checks before sending

1. Ten years of statements were used, or the Gaps line says why fewer.
2. The ROIC quoted is named (hand-built or FactSet) and the two are reconciled in one line.
3. Every moat checklist item has evidence or a stated gap.
4. One-offs are counted by recurrence, and the EBITA rebuild is shown.
5. The buyback return is computed at the prices paid, net of issuance.
6. "What the price implies" precedes the valuation and the opening section reads consistently with it.
7. Terminal value share, implied terminal multiple and the bridge per share are all shown.
8. Probabilities sum to 100 and are anchored to a reference class.
9. Kill criteria have dates or observable thresholds.
10. No rating word. Every table, including the catalysts and risks tables, has Basis and Source columns, and every figure in prose has a citation or a basis word.
11. The special case was applied if the company is a bank, a cyclical, high growth or a conglomerate.

## Hand-offs

- The user wants only the thesis and its claims: `bigdata-thesis`. Only the valuation: `bigdata-valuation`. Only the moat: `bigdata-moat`.
- After delivering, make one offer: save the report to the user's Bigdata.com account, or turn the user's preferences for this report into a skill of their own. Act only on a clear yes.

# Working with Bigdata.com

Guidance for using the Bigdata.com tools well. It describes approaches, not arguments: each tool's own description is the authority on what it takes and returns, so read it before the first call. Tool names below are the base names; a host may add a prefix to them.

Use judgment. A one-line question needs one or two calls. A research task needs a plan, several calls, and a second look when the first results leave a gap.

## Which data answers which question

| The question is about | Start with | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| What happened, what was said, why something moved | `bigdata_search` | News, filings, transcripts, broker research, podcasts, expert interviews and the user's own documents. Returns cited excerpts. |
| One company's numbers: financials, estimates, ratings, price targets, ownership | `bigdata_company_tearsheet` | Needs the company resolved first. Works for private companies too, with different content. |
| How the media sees a company, and why | `bigdata_sentiment_tearsheet` | Score, attention and a cited narrative. |
| Several companies at a glance: price, daily move, earnings surprise, targets, sentiment | `bigdata_portfolio_tearsheet` | One row per company. Then write a short read of the movers. |
| News across a list of companies | `bigdata_watchlist_search` | Gives every name its share of results. A plain search lets the most-covered names crowd out the rest. |
| Markets today: indexes, sectors, commodities, rates, currencies, crypto, factors | `bigdata_market_tearsheet` | One call covers all of it. |
| One country's economy | `bigdata_country_tearsheet` | Growth, inflation, rates, indices, currency, and a G7 comparison. |
| An ETF | `bigdata_etf_tearsheet` | Needs the ETF resolved first. |
| What is coming up: earnings dates, conferences, IPOs, economic releases | `bigdata_events_calendar` | Company events and economic releases are two different calendars. |
| Companies that match criteria the user describes | `bigdata_screen_companies` | Then use the portfolio tearsheet for current figures. |
| Credit risk signals | `bigdata_get_credit_factor`, `bigdata_screen_credit_factor` | One company, or a ranking across many. |
| A calculation, a series, a chart | `bigdata_computer` | Compute rather than doing arithmetic by hand. |
| The user's own documents and feeds | `bigdata_list_connectors`, `bigdata_list_tags`, `bigdata_list_documents` | Discover what they have, then search or read it. |
| Which publications Bigdata.com covers | `bigdata_find_sources` | For "do you cover the FT?" and for source filters. |
| The user's subscription and data packages | `bigdata_help` | |

Most tasks combine two or three of these: numbers from a tearsheet, the story behind them from search, the next event from the calendar.

## Resolve the company first

- Resolve every company, ticker, ETF or fund to its Bigdata.com entity before calling a tool that needs an entity id: tearsheets, the calendar, watchlists, fast searches with entity filters. Use `find_securities` for names and tickers, `get_securities` for ISIN, CUSIP, SEDOL or exchange listings, and `find_entities` for people, places, products and organizations that are not companies.
- Resolve several names in parallel, one call each.
- Take whether a company is public or private from the lookup result, never from training knowledge.
- If the top match is not clearly the company the user meant, look at the other matches, then ask.
- Resolve once. Reuse ids already confirmed in the conversation.
- A smart search resolves company names itself, so a lookup only to prepare a search is not needed.

## Search well

- **One topic, one period, one group of companies per search.** A combined query shares a fixed number of excerpts across everything it asks, so each part comes back thin. "Nvidia earnings and partnerships in 2024 and 2025" is four searches.
- **Write the query as a sentence,** not a list of keywords: "What did Nike say about inventory on its latest earnings call?"
- **Keep the user's time words.** "Last quarter", "yesterday", "FY2024" go into the query as said. Do not add dates the user or the results did not give.
- **List the angles first.** For a broad question, plan one search per angle. One relevant-looking result is not a reason to stop.
- **Pass a scope hint only when the user gave one:** their own files, a source, a tag, a broker.
- **The open web is a last resort,** for things outside Bigdata.com's content (a product page, a blog), and the user is told when an answer comes from it. News is not one of them.

## When a smart search comes back weak

Smart search reports how it read the query: the entity, period, source type and document type it chose, and how many excerpts matched. Read that report before retrying.

- **It read the query wrong** (wrong company, wrong period, wrong document type): run another smart search with a clearer query.
- **It read the query right, but the excerpts are empty, thin or off-topic:** retry in fast mode with the filters the report gives, and change only the query text. Simplify the wording, or phrase it the way the document would ("guidance" rather than "fiscal Q1 2026 outlook"). This keeps the retry on the right company, period and source instead of drifting.
- Prefer this smart-to-fast retry over a second smart search whenever the report already has the right filters.

## When to read the full document

A search returns ranked excerpts, not whole documents. Fetch the full document, with an id a search returned, when:

- the user asks for a document itself ("summarize the 10-K", "what did the CFO say in Q&A"),
- the answer depends on context the excerpts cut off (a table, a guidance range, a risk factor's full wording),
- one document carries the task (an earnings call for a digest, a filing for a risk review).

Do not fetch documents to answer what excerpts already answer. Never invent a document id or a URL.

## Lists of companies

When the user names companies they own or follow, resolve them all, then use the portfolio tearsheet for numbers and the watchlist search for news. When they refer to a saved list ("my watchlist", "my holdings"), load it rather than asking them to name the companies again.

## Saving to the user's Bigdata.com account

Saving changes the user's account, so offer it in one line and act only on a clear yes. Each fits a different moment:

- **A watchlist,** when the user named companies they own or follow. Later runs can start from it instead of the user listing the names again.
- **A monitor,** when the user wants to hear when something changes on a subject. Offer a test run on past data before turning it on.
- **The deliverable,** after a substantial one (a memo, brief, preview, comparison or screen), so later searches can find it. Not after a quick answer. Tell the user it becomes searchable once processed, not at once.

## When a tool returns an error

Read it. Most errors name the argument that was wrong; fix it and retry once. If it fails again, tell the user what could not be retrieved.

## The company tearsheet in detail

The company tearsheet is large. Ask for the sections the task needs with the tool's `sections` argument (its values are listed below), and split a full pull into two or three calls so no response is too big to use. The `interval` argument chooses five quarters (the default) or five fiscal years of statements; there is no period offset, so ten years of statements is not available from this tool.

| Section value | What it carries |
|---|---|
| `company_overview` | Profile, description, the real-time quote and price performance (52-week range, moving averages, price changes over standard windows) |
| `c_level_leadership` | Executives, board composition, management stats (needs FactSet access) |
| `financial_statements` | FactSet income statement, balance sheet and cash flow for five periods, with stock-based compensation split out, gross and net PP&E, goodwill and intangibles, invested capital, capex, buybacks, dividends |
| `financial_ratios` | Gross margin, P/E, P/B, debt ratios, ROIC, ROE, cash conversion cycle, Altman Z, Piotroski (trailing twelve months) |
| `key_metrics` | Market cap, enterprise value, EV/EBITDA, free cash flow yield, net debt (trailing twelve months) |
| `analyst_estimates` | Consensus for sales, EBIT, EBITDA, EPS, free cash flow, capex and long-term growth, with the actual where reported, the surprise in percent, and the company's guidance (low, mid, high) where the company gives it |
| `analyst_ratings` | Rating counts and price targets (consensus, median, high, low) |
| `latest_earnings` | The last reported quarter against consensus |
| `earnings_calendar` | The next earnings date |
| `revenue_segmentation` | Revenue by product and by geography |
| `fund_trends_history` | 13F holders, top buyers and sellers, position changes, options activity |
| `dividends`, `esg_performance`, `hiring_trends`, `mergers_acquisitions` | As named; M&A needs FactSet access |

The tool's own description says to omit `sections` for a general tearsheet request. A skill that needs three sections for a specific step is such a request: pass them.

Rules that follow from the data:

- Five periods come back per call, quarterly or annual by `interval`. For a ten-year view, use the annual statements and say in the Gaps line that the series stops at five years.
- The FactSet ROIC field and a hand-built ROIC differ by definition (tax rate, goodwill, leases). Say which one the report quotes and never mix them in one table.
- Not in Bigdata.com: a cost of capital or WACC, short interest, options data, intraday prices. State the cost of capital as an assumption with its basis and show a sensitivity. Say in the Gaps line when positioning data would have mattered.
- Consensus has a vintage: the date in the estimates section. Quote it next to any consensus figure, with the number of estimates when given.
- Price series and anything that needs more than a few steps of arithmetic go through `bigdata_computer`.

## Transcripts and guidance

- Guidance for the next quarter is given on the call for the quarter just reported. To read the guidance for Q1 FY2027, fetch the Q4 FY2026 call, never a later one. A smart search that resolves to a call that has not happened yet has read the period wrong; retry in fast mode with the reporting period filter set to the quarter of the call you need (fiscal year and quarter).
- Quote guidance verbatim with its range and the date of the call, then the consensus next to it.
- Research notes and news carry sell-side reactions (target changes, rating changes, the reasons). Until broker research is available in the account, search for those when a skill needs the Street's view, and label them as press or research summaries.
- Use `reporting_periods` (fiscal year and fiscal quarter) with a `document_type` of TRANSCRIPT and subtype EARNINGS_CALL on fast searches, so the period is fixed rather than inferred; the `sections` filter picks the prepared remarks (MANAGEMENT-DISCUSSION) or the Q&A (QUESTION-ANSWER).

## The skill slug

Pass `plugin_slug` with the skill's name on every Bigdata.com call that accepts it. It tells Bigdata.com which skill is running, which is how usage per skill is counted. The value is the skill's `name` field, for example `bigdata-earnings-preview`.
# Output standard

Every Bigdata.com skill writes to this standard, so a reader who has seen one report knows where to look in the next. The reader is a portfolio manager or analyst who wants the evidence, the arithmetic behind it and what would change the reading, in plain language. Follow the user's own structure, length or format when they gave one, and keep the citations, the Gaps line and the footer in every case.

## The frame

1. **Header.** The title names the subject, the ticker and the job ("Micron (MU) earnings preview: Q1 FY2027, reports 17 Dec 2026 after market"). Under it, one line: "Data as of:" with the date of the price used, the vintage of the estimates, the latest fiscal period in the statements and the date of the newest document read.
2. **The answer first.** Four to eight sentences in prose that say what the evidence shows, what the price implies where that applies, and what would change the reading. No heading called "Executive summary"; call it what it is ("The setup", "The view", "What happened").
3. **The body** in the sections the skill defines, in its order.
4. **What would change this view.** Two to five conditions, each observable and dated where possible.
5. **Gaps.** What Bigdata.com could not answer, in one or two lines. Never fill a gap from memory or the open web without saying so in this line.
6. **Sources**, then the footer, verbatim.

## Numbers

- Every figure carries its unit, currency and period, and consensus figures carry their vintage and the number of estimates when the tearsheet gives it.
- Tables have a **Basis** column and a **Source** column. Basis is one of four words: *reported* (taken from a document or a data set, with a citation), *derived* (computed from reported figures; name the formula or the fields once, in a note under the table or in the Data line), *assumed* (an input the analyst chose, with its basis), *judgment*.
- In prose, mark a derived or assumed figure the first time it appears ("implied growth of 4.5 percent a year, derived at an assumed 9 percent cost of capital"). Reported figures need only their citation.
- Assumptions appear once, in a table or an Assumptions line, with the reason for each value and a sensitivity where the result depends on it.
- Historical base rates are labelled with their sample and period ("top 1,000 global companies by market cap, 1950 to 2015, inflation-adjusted") and never presented as current facts. Dated figures from the method files carry "(verify)".
- Ranges, not points, for forecasts and values. Probabilities sum to 100 and say where the weights came from.
- Compute with `bigdata_computer` or the host's code execution when the arithmetic has more than a few steps, and show the working for anything a reader would want to check.

## Citations

- Cite inline with numbers in square brackets right after the claim: "guided to $9.6bn at the midpoint [3]". One number per source; reuse the number for a source cited twice.
- The **Sources** section lists every number once, in the server's link format: `[3] [Micron Q4 FY2026 earnings call - Sep 24, 2026](url)`, with the attribution URL the tool result gave. Never invent a URL or a document id.
- Figures computed from Bigdata.com data sets that have no document behind them (prices, estimates, statements, screens) are covered by one **Data** line after the numbered sources: "Data: Bigdata.com company tearsheet for Micron, FactSet fundamentals and consensus estimates, retrieved Oct 23, 2026."
- A claim with no source and no Basis label does not go in the report. This applies to numbers inside sentences as much as to tables: a figure in prose carries its citation number or its basis word (derived, assumed) in the same sentence.

## No recommendation

The report describes the balance of evidence and what would change it. It never gives a buy, hold, sell, overweight, underweight, accumulate, avoid or similar call, a rating, a stance line, a price target of its own, or a position size. When a user asks "is it a buy", answer with what the price assumes, what the evidence says about that, and what would change the reading. The disclaimer below promises this, and a call would contradict it.

## Size

| Skill | Length |
|---|---|
| quick-take | one page |
| company-brief, stock-move, catalysts, watchlist, markets-today | one to two pages |
| earnings-preview, earnings-review, valuation, comps, scenarios, earnings-quality, moat, capital-allocation, risk, credit, screen | two to four pages |
| deep-dive, thesis, sector, theme, country, macro-compare, deal-analysis, special-situations | four to eight pages |

A narrow question gets a direct answer in the skill's method with the relevant table and the sources, not the full report. The footer stays.

## Language

- Plain sentences, active verbs, the company and the ticker by name. Buy-side vocabulary is fine for this reader; define an uncommon term on first use.
- No hype adjectives, no "robust", "compelling", "significant" without a number, no exclamation marks, no emojis.
- Facts, then what they mean, then what would change the reading. Keep the three apart.
- Markdown by default: headings, tables for anything tabular, short paragraphs. Offer a Word document for a formal deliverable when the host can create files.

## Footer

Reproduce the two blocks below verbatim after Sources in every user-facing deliverable, including a one-line answer. The report ends on the disclaimer. The one offer a skill makes after delivery (save a watchlist, a monitor or the report; build a skill) is conversation, not report: put it in a separate short line after a blank line, so the deliverable itself still ends on the disclaimer.

**Powered by Bigdata.com** - https://bigdata.com

This output is for informational and research-assistance purposes only. It does **not** constitute investment, legal, tax, accounting, or other professional advice, and it is **not** a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any security or instrument or to pursue any strategy. Information may be incomplete, estimated, delayed, or inaccurate. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Verify material facts independently and consult qualified advisors before making decisions.

# Working with Bigdata.com

Guidance for using the Bigdata.com tools well. It describes approaches, not arguments: each tool's own description is the authority on what it takes and returns, so read it before the first call. Tool names below are the base names; a host may add a prefix to them.

Use judgment. A one-line question needs one or two calls. A research task needs a plan, several calls, and a second look when the first results leave a gap.

## Which data answers which question

| The question is about | Start with | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| What happened, what was said, why something moved | `bigdata_search` | News, filings, transcripts, broker research, podcasts, expert interviews and the user's own documents. Returns cited excerpts. |
| One company's numbers: financials, estimates, ratings, price targets, ownership | `bigdata_company_tearsheet` | Needs the company resolved first. Works for private companies too, with different content. |
| How the media sees a company, and why | `bigdata_sentiment_tearsheet` | Score, attention and a cited narrative. |
| Several companies at a glance: price, daily move, earnings surprise, targets, sentiment | `bigdata_portfolio_tearsheet` | One row per company. Then write a short read of the movers. |
| News across a list of companies | `bigdata_watchlist_search` | Gives every name its share of results. A plain search lets the most-covered names crowd out the rest. |
| Markets today: indexes, sectors, commodities, rates, currencies, crypto, factors | `bigdata_market_tearsheet` | One call covers all of it. |
| One country's economy | `bigdata_country_tearsheet` | Growth, inflation, rates, indices, currency, and a G7 comparison. |
| An ETF | `bigdata_etf_tearsheet` | Needs the ETF resolved first. |
| What is coming up: earnings dates, conferences, IPOs, economic releases | `bigdata_events_calendar` | Company events and economic releases are two different calendars. |
| Companies that match criteria the user describes | `bigdata_screen_companies` | Then use the portfolio tearsheet for current figures. |
| Credit risk signals | `bigdata_get_credit_factor`, `bigdata_screen_credit_factor` | One company, or a ranking across many. |
| A calculation, a series, a chart | `bigdata_computer` | Compute rather than doing arithmetic by hand. |
| The user's own documents and feeds | `bigdata_list_connectors`, `bigdata_list_tags`, `bigdata_list_documents` | Discover what they have, then search or read it. |
| Which publications Bigdata.com covers | `bigdata_find_sources` | For "do you cover the FT?" and for source filters. |
| The user's subscription and data packages | `bigdata_help` | |

Most tasks combine two or three of these: numbers from a tearsheet, the story behind them from search, the next event from the calendar.

## Resolve the company first

- Resolve every company, ticker, ETF or fund to its Bigdata.com entity before calling a tool that needs an entity id: tearsheets, the calendar, watchlists, fast searches with entity filters. Use `find_securities` for names and tickers, `get_securities` for ISIN, CUSIP, SEDOL or exchange listings, and `find_entities` for people, places, products and organizations that are not companies.
- Resolve several names in parallel, one call each.
- Take whether a company is public or private from the lookup result, never from training knowledge.
- If the top match is not clearly the company the user meant, look at the other matches, then ask.
- Resolve once. Reuse ids already confirmed in the conversation.
- A smart search resolves company names itself, so a lookup only to prepare a search is not needed.

## Search well

- **One topic, one period, one group of companies per search.** A combined query shares a fixed number of excerpts across everything it asks, so each part comes back thin. "Nvidia earnings and partnerships in 2024 and 2025" is four searches.
- **Write the query as a sentence,** not a list of keywords: "What did Nike say about inventory on its latest earnings call?"
- **Keep the user's time words.** "Last quarter", "yesterday", "FY2024" go into the query as said. Do not add dates the user or the results did not give.
- **List the angles first.** For a broad question, plan one search per angle. One relevant-looking result is not a reason to stop.
- **Pass a scope hint only when the user gave one:** their own files, a source, a tag, a broker.
- **The open web is a last resort,** for things outside Bigdata.com's content (a product page, a blog), and the user is told when an answer comes from it. News is not one of them.

## When a smart search comes back weak

Smart search reports how it read the query: the entity, period, source type and document type it chose, and how many excerpts matched. Read that report before retrying.

- **It read the query wrong** (wrong company, wrong period, wrong document type): run another smart search with a clearer query.
- **It read the query right, but the excerpts are empty, thin or off-topic:** retry in fast mode with the filters the report gives, and change only the query text. Simplify the wording, or phrase it the way the document would ("guidance" rather than "fiscal Q1 2026 outlook"). This keeps the retry on the right company, period and source instead of drifting.
- Prefer this smart-to-fast retry over a second smart search whenever the report already has the right filters.

## When to read the full document

A search returns ranked excerpts, not whole documents. Fetch the full document, with an id a search returned, when:

- the user asks for a document itself ("summarize the 10-K", "what did the CFO say in Q&A"),
- the answer depends on context the excerpts cut off (a table, a guidance range, a risk factor's full wording),
- one document carries the task (an earnings call for a digest, a filing for a risk review).

Do not fetch documents to answer what excerpts already answer. Never invent a document id or a URL.

## Lists of companies

When the user names companies they own or follow, resolve them all, then use the portfolio tearsheet for numbers and the watchlist search for news. When they refer to a saved list ("my watchlist", "my holdings"), load it rather than asking them to name the companies again.

## Saving to the user's Bigdata.com account

Saving changes the user's account, so offer it in one line and act only on a clear yes. Each fits a different moment:

- **A watchlist,** when the user named companies they own or follow. Later runs can start from it instead of the user listing the names again.
- **A monitor,** when the user wants to hear when something changes on a subject. Offer a test run on past data before turning it on.
- **The deliverable,** after a substantial one (a memo, brief, preview, comparison or screen), so later searches can find it. Not after a quick answer. Tell the user it becomes searchable once processed, not at once.

## When a tool returns an error

Read it. Most errors name the argument that was wrong; fix it and retry once. If it fails again, tell the user what could not be retrieved.

## The company tearsheet in detail

The company tearsheet is large. Ask for the sections the task needs with the tool's `sections` argument (its values are listed below), and split a full pull into two or three calls so no response is too big to use. The `interval` argument chooses five quarters (the default) or five fiscal years of statements; there is no period offset, so ten years of statements is not available from this tool.

| Section value | What it carries |
|---|---|
| `company_overview` | Profile, description, the real-time quote and price performance (52-week range, moving averages, price changes over standard windows) |
| `c_level_leadership` | Executives, board composition, management stats (needs FactSet access) |
| `financial_statements` | FactSet income statement, balance sheet and cash flow for five periods, with stock-based compensation split out, gross and net PP&E, goodwill and intangibles, invested capital, capex, buybacks, dividends |
| `financial_ratios` | Gross margin, P/E, P/B, debt ratios, ROIC, ROE, cash conversion cycle, Altman Z, Piotroski (trailing twelve months) |
| `key_metrics` | Market cap, enterprise value, EV/EBITDA, free cash flow yield, net debt (trailing twelve months) |
| `analyst_estimates` | Consensus for sales, EBIT, EBITDA, EPS, free cash flow, capex and long-term growth, with the actual where reported, the surprise in percent, and the company's guidance (low, mid, high) where the company gives it |
| `analyst_ratings` | Rating counts and price targets (consensus, median, high, low) |
| `latest_earnings` | The last reported quarter against consensus |
| `earnings_calendar` | The next earnings date |
| `revenue_segmentation` | Revenue by product and by geography |
| `fund_trends_history` | 13F holders, top buyers and sellers, position changes, options activity |
| `dividends`, `esg_performance`, `hiring_trends`, `mergers_acquisitions` | As named; M&A needs FactSet access |

The tool's own description says to omit `sections` for a general tearsheet request. A skill that needs three sections for a specific step is such a request: pass them.

Rules that follow from the data:

- Five periods come back per call, quarterly or annual by `interval`. For a ten-year view, use the annual statements and say in the Gaps line that the series stops at five years.
- The FactSet ROIC field and a hand-built ROIC differ by definition (tax rate, goodwill, leases). Say which one the report quotes and never mix them in one table.
- Not in Bigdata.com: a cost of capital or WACC, short interest, options data, intraday prices. State the cost of capital as an assumption with its basis and show a sensitivity. Say in the Gaps line when positioning data would have mattered.
- Consensus has a vintage: the date in the estimates section. Quote it next to any consensus figure, with the number of estimates when given.
- Price series and anything that needs more than a few steps of arithmetic go through `bigdata_computer`.

## Transcripts and guidance

- Guidance for the next quarter is given on the call for the quarter just reported. To read the guidance for Q1 FY2027, fetch the Q4 FY2026 call, never a later one. A smart search that resolves to a call that has not happened yet has read the period wrong; retry in fast mode with the reporting period filter set to the quarter of the call you need (fiscal year and quarter).
- Quote guidance verbatim with its range and the date of the call, then the consensus next to it.
- Research notes and news carry sell-side reactions (target changes, rating changes, the reasons). Until broker research is available in the account, search for those when a skill needs the Street's view, and label them as press or research summaries.
- Use `reporting_periods` (fiscal year and fiscal quarter) with a `document_type` of TRANSCRIPT and subtype EARNINGS_CALL on fast searches, so the period is fixed rather than inferred; the `sections` filter picks the prepared remarks (MANAGEMENT-DISCUSSION) or the Q&A (QUESTION-ANSWER).

## The skill slug

Pass `plugin_slug` with the skill's name on every Bigdata.com call that accepts it. It tells Bigdata.com which skill is running, which is how usage per skill is counted. The value is the skill's `name` field, for example `bigdata-earnings-preview`.
# Output standard

Every Bigdata.com skill writes to this standard, so a reader who has seen one report knows where to look in the next. The reader is a portfolio manager or analyst who wants the evidence, the arithmetic behind it and what would change the reading, in plain language. Follow the user's own structure, length or format when they gave one, and keep the citations, the Gaps line and the footer in every case.

## The frame

1. **Header.** The title names the subject, the ticker and the job ("Micron (MU) earnings preview: Q1 FY2027, reports 17 Dec 2026 after market"). Under it, one line: "Data as of:" with the date of the price used, the vintage of the estimates, the latest fiscal period in the statements and the date of the newest document read.
2. **The answer first.** Four to eight sentences in prose that say what the evidence shows, what the price implies where that applies, and what would change the reading. No heading called "Executive summary"; call it what it is ("The setup", "The view", "What happened").
3. **The body** in the sections the skill defines, in its order.
4. **What would change this view.** Two to five conditions, each observable and dated where possible.
5. **Gaps.** What Bigdata.com could not answer, in one or two lines. Never fill a gap from memory or the open web without saying so in this line.
6. **Sources**, then the footer, verbatim.

## Numbers

- Every figure carries its unit, currency and period, and consensus figures carry their vintage and the number of estimates when the tearsheet gives it.
- Tables have a **Basis** column and a **Source** column. Basis is one of four words: *reported* (taken from a document or a data set, with a citation), *derived* (computed from reported figures; name the formula or the fields once, in a note under the table or in the Data line), *assumed* (an input the analyst chose, with its basis), *judgment*.
- In prose, mark a derived or assumed figure the first time it appears ("implied growth of 4.5 percent a year, derived at an assumed 9 percent cost of capital"). Reported figures need only their citation.
- Assumptions appear once, in a table or an Assumptions line, with the reason for each value and a sensitivity where the result depends on it.
- Historical base rates are labelled with their sample and period ("top 1,000 global companies by market cap, 1950 to 2015, inflation-adjusted") and never presented as current facts. Dated figures from the method files carry "(verify)".
- Ranges, not points, for forecasts and values. Probabilities sum to 100 and say where the weights came from.
- Compute with `bigdata_computer` or the host's code execution when the arithmetic has more than a few steps, and show the working for anything a reader would want to check.

## Citations

- Cite inline with numbers in square brackets right after the claim: "guided to $9.6bn at the midpoint [3]". One number per source; reuse the number for a source cited twice.
- The **Sources** section lists every number once, in the server's link format: `[3] [Micron Q4 FY2026 earnings call - Sep 24, 2026](url)`, with the attribution URL the tool result gave. Never invent a URL or a document id.
- Figures computed from Bigdata.com data sets that have no document behind them (prices, estimates, statements, screens) are covered by one **Data** line after the numbered sources: "Data: Bigdata.com company tearsheet for Micron, FactSet fundamentals and consensus estimates, retrieved Oct 23, 2026."
- A claim with no source and no Basis label does not go in the report. This applies to numbers inside sentences as much as to tables: a figure in prose carries its citation number or its basis word (derived, assumed) in the same sentence.

## No recommendation

The report describes the balance of evidence and what would change it. It never gives a buy, hold, sell, overweight, underweight, accumulate, avoid or similar call, a rating, a stance line, a price target of its own, or a position size. When a user asks "is it a buy", answer with what the price assumes, what the evidence says about that, and what would change the reading. The disclaimer below promises this, and a call would contradict it.

## Size

| Skill | Length |
|---|---|
| quick-take | one page |
| company-brief, stock-move, catalysts, watchlist, markets-today | one to two pages |
| earnings-preview, earnings-review, valuation, comps, scenarios, earnings-quality, moat, capital-allocation, risk, credit, screen | two to four pages |
| deep-dive, thesis, sector, theme, country, macro-compare, deal-analysis, special-situations | four to eight pages |

A narrow question gets a direct answer in the skill's method with the relevant table and the sources, not the full report. The footer stays.

## Language

- Plain sentences, active verbs, the company and the ticker by name. Buy-side vocabulary is fine for this reader; define an uncommon term on first use.
- No hype adjectives, no "robust", "compelling", "significant" without a number, no exclamation marks, no emojis.
- Facts, then what they mean, then what would change the reading. Keep the three apart.
- Markdown by default: headings, tables for anything tabular, short paragraphs. Offer a Word document for a formal deliverable when the host can create files.

## Footer

Reproduce the two blocks below verbatim after Sources in every user-facing deliverable, including a one-line answer. The report ends on the disclaimer. The one offer a skill makes after delivery (save a watchlist, a monitor or the report; build a skill) is conversation, not report: put it in a separate short line after a blank line, so the deliverable itself still ends on the disclaimer.

# Return on invested capital

This method answers what the company earns on the capital its operations use, how that compares with its cost of capital, and where that return is heading. ROIC moves by a factor of two or more on definitions alone (Procter and Gamble 2006: 10.6 percent with goodwill in capital, 26.2 percent without; Damodaran 2007, pp. 43-45), so the method fixes each choice, states it, and applies it identically to peers. Starting ROIC is already in the price; a stock moves on changes in returns against expectations (Mauboussin and Callahan 2013, Economic Returns, pp. 2-7). The output is a definition line, a ROIC bridge, a spread over a stated cost of capital and a reasoned reversion path, never a rating.

## When a skill loads this file

Whenever a report states a return on capital, a spread, a moat or a fade assumption: deep dives, valuation, moat, earnings quality, capital allocation, thesis and sector work. A narrow question ("what is the ROIC") gets the definition line, ROIC with and without goodwill, the FactSet field and the spread, not the full bridge. Banks and insurers use adjusted ROE (see Interpretation and limits).

The output is a definition line, a ROIC bridge, a spread over a stated cost of capital and a reasoned reversion path, never a rating.

## When a skill loads this file

Whenever a report states a return on capital, a spread, a moat or a fade assumption: deep dives, valuation, moat, earnings quality, capital allocation, thesis and sector work. A narrow question ("what is the ROIC") gets the definition line, ROIC with and without goodwill, the FactSet field and the spread, not the full bridge. Banks and insurers use adjusted ROE (see Interpretation and limits).

## Inputs

| Input | Where in Bigdata.com | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue, EBIT, amortization of acquired intangibles, pretax income, tax expense, interest expense and income, non-operating income, R&D | `bigdata_company_tearsheet`, section `financial_statements, financial_ratios, key_metrics` (income statement), five fiscal periods per call | reported |
| Receivables, inventory, prepaid, payables, accruals, deferred revenue, net and gross PP&E, goodwill and intangibles, cash and securities, debt, lease liabilities where reported, equity, minority interest, invested capital field | `financial_statements, financial_ratios, key_metrics` (balance sheet) | reported |
| FactSet ROIC, margins, cash conversion cycle | `financial_statements, financial_ratios, key_metrics` (ratios) | reported |
| Revenue by segment | `revenue_segmentation` (revenue only, no segment capital) | reported |
| Tax reconciliation, lease note, deferred tax note, R&D, restructuring and impairment history, segment assets | `bigdata_search` on filings, then `bigdata_fetch_document` for the note | reported |
| Risk-free rate, equity risk premium, beta, credit spread, target weights | Not in Bigdata.com. Beta can be computed with `bigdata_computer` where it returns a price series; otherwise cite an industry beta | assumed |

For a ten-year series request earlier periods if the tool allows it; otherwise work with five and say so in Gaps.

## Procedure

1. **State the definition.** One line naming: tax method (operating or cash), average or opening capital, goodwill in or out, leases, R&D, the excess cash rule. Done when the line sits under every ROIC table and peers use the same line.
2. **Build NOPAT.** EBITA = EBIT plus amortization of acquired intangibles. Apply the operating tax rate from the tax reconciliation note: statutory plus state or local rate, plus recurring operating items (foreign rate differences, credits that scale with revenue), excluding one-offs and the interest tax shield (McKinsey ch. 7, 25). Never use reported tax or the effective rate: they contain the interest shield, which WACC already counts (Damodaran 2007, p. 8). Optional cash-tax row: subtract the increase in net operating deferred tax liabilities (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, pp. 2-3). Done when NOPAT ties to the tax note and the rate is written down.
3. **Classify unusual items.** One-time: remove. Recurring at intervals (restructuring every three years): spread per year. Recurring but volatile: average. Recurring with sign flips (currency translation): ignore (Damodaran 2007, pp. 37-39). Count how many of the last five years carry a "one-time" charge; recurring ones are costs. Done when each item has a class.
4. **Build invested capital from the operating side.** Operating working capital (operating cash, receivables, inventory, prepaid, less payables, accruals, deferred revenue, taxes payable; no excess cash, no interest-bearing items) plus net PP&E plus goodwill and acquired intangibles plus other net operating assets (McKinsey ch. 7). Keep an item only if the company could not earn the same NOPAT without it (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, p. 5). Done when every balance-sheet line is classed operating, non-operating or financing.
5. **Build it from the financing side and reconcile.** Debt plus lease liabilities plus unfunded pensions plus equity plus minority interest, less excess cash and non-operating assets. A gap between the two sides is a missed item. Compare with the tearsheet invested capital field. Done when the two sides agree or the difference is explained.
6. **Strip excess cash.** Operating cash allowance: 2 percent of sales for steady companies, 5 percent for less predictable or faster-growing ones (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, pp. 6-7; McKinsey ch. 7 uses 2 percent). Remove the same amount from equity and keep interest on cash out of NOPAT. Done when the allowance and the amount removed are shown.
7. **Show ROIC with and without goodwill.** Without goodwill and acquired intangibles measures the operating business and is the basis for peer comparison; with them measures the return on all capital raised, premiums included (McKinsey ch. 8; Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, pp. 7-8). Add cumulative impairments and amortization back to goodwill. Judge an acquisition by its net present value, not by ROIC (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, fn. 12). Done when both columns appear.
8. **Treat leases.** State whether the statements capitalize leases (ASC 842 and IFRS 16 put most leases on balance sheet from 2019; verify for the company and the period). If capitalized, add the implied interest (prior-year lease liability x pre-tax cost of secured debt) to EBITA and keep the liability in capital and in debt. For earlier periods, estimate the leased asset with the formula below. The WACC debt weight changes too. Done when ROIC is shown before and after.
9. **Capitalize R&D when it is material.** Advertising or customer acquisition only with evidence of a multi-year benefit (Damodaran 2007, pp. 27-28). Choose an amortizable life (pharma about 10 years, software short), build the research asset, replace R&D expense with amortization in EBITA and add the asset to capital. Operating taxes do not change because R&D is deductible in full (McKinsey ch. 28). Say so if the R&D history is shorter than the life. Done when the life and the adjusted ROIC are shown.
10. **Compute and decompose.** Headline ROIC on average of opening and closing capital (McKinsey ch. 8); show the opening-capital variant (Damodaran 2007, p. 7). Decompose into (1 - operating tax rate) x EBITA margin x capital turnover over five to ten years, with working capital in days. High margin points to a consumer advantage, high turnover to a production advantage (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, pp. 12-14). Segment ROIC needs segment assets from the filing. Done when the series and the decomposition are tabled.
11. **Compute ROIIC, the cost of capital and the spread.** ROIIC over one, three and five years. WACC from the build in `references/valuation.md`, shown as prevailing and normalized, each labelled (Mauboussin and Callahan 2013, Cost of Capital, pp. 22-25). Economic profit in currency. Done when spread and economic profit sit next to ROIC for every year.
12. **Set the reversion path** with the fade table and persistence figures below, and give the reason from the competitive evidence in `references/industry-structure.md`. Done when the path names a starting spread, years, an endpoint and the reason.

## Formulas

- ROIC = NOPAT / average invested capital. NOPAT = EBITA x (1 - operating tax rate).
- Cash NOPAT = EBITA - (operating taxes - increase in net operating deferred tax liability).
- Economic profit = invested capital x (ROIC - WACC) = NOPAT - WACC x invested capital. Use one capital definition for both terms (McKinsey ch. 6).
- ROIC = (1 - t) x (EBITA / revenue) x (revenue / invested capital). Days of an item = 365 x item / revenue (inventory and payables on COGS).
- Growth identity: g = ROIC x investment rate; investment rate = net investment / NOPAT; FCF = NOPAT - net investment (McKinsey ch. 2).
- Value driver: value = NOPAT(t+1) x (1 - g / RONIC) / (WACC - g), RONIC = return on new invested capital (McKinsey ch. 2 and 10).
- ROIIC, one year = (NOPAT(t) - NOPAT(t-1)) / (IC(t-1) - IC(t-2)) (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, p. 10). Rolling n-year form (derived): (NOPAT(t) - NOPAT(t-n)) / (IC(t-1) - IC(t-n-1)); use n = 3 and 5 when investment is lumpy.
- Research asset = sum over t = -(n-1) to 0 of R&D(t) x (n + t) / n, n = amortizable life; current-year R&D is unamortized. Adjusted EBIT = EBIT + R&D - amortization of the research asset (Damodaran 2007, p. 20).
- Leased asset value(t-1) = rental expense(t) / (kd + 1 / asset life); kd = cost of secured debt, asset life = PP&E / annual depreciation (McKinsey ch. 27).
- WACC = D/V x kd x (1 - Tm) + E/V x ke, target market-value weights; ke = rf + beta x ERP.
- Unlevered beta: beta_u = beta_L / [1 + (1 - T) x D/E] (Mauboussin and Callahan 2013, pp. 14-19); McKinsey's form without the tax term, beta_L = beta_u x (1 + D/E), assumes the tax shield carries operating risk (ch. 11). State which one is used. Adjusted beta = 0.67 x raw + 0.33.
- Expected value of a persistent metric in four years = sector mean + r x (current - sector mean), r = four-year persistence (Mauboussin, How to Model Reversion to the Mean, 2013).

## Interpretation and limits

- Two tests for advantage: ROIC above the cost of capital and above peers, over a full cycle (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, pp. 12-14). Value needs the spread and the capital deployed at it, so judge economic profit, not ROIC alone.
- Show ROIC, ROIIC and RONIC for every forecast year. Forecast ROIC stays near today's level, trends to the industry median, or trends to WACC, with a stated reason (McKinsey ch. 9). Fading a top-quintile company to WACC is usually too conservative given the transition table; a recovery for a low-ROIC company needs a specific cause.
- Never compare ROIIC with WACC; a high ROIIC can be operating leverage. Use it to spot change: Dell's average ROIC stayed high while marginal returns swung widely (Damodaran 2007, p. 51).
- Flag ROIC lifted by write-offs that shrink capital (a $10bn asset earning $0.5bn is 5 percent; write off half and it reads 10 percent; Damodaran 2007, pp. 37-39). Buybacks lift ROE, not ROIC.
- Flag any jump in capital turnover and any forecast that implies negative capex (McKinsey ch. 9, 13).
- Never put the FactSet ROIC field and a hand-built ROIC in one comparison; name which one each line quotes. Apply identical adjustments to every peer.
- Does not apply to banks and insurers: use ROE on adjusted net income against the cost of equity, decomposed with leverage (Mauboussin and Callahan 2014, p. 11). Captive finance arms: separate them and use ROE on allocated equity; a blended figure is meaningless (McKinsey ch. 7, 12). Negative NOPAT or negative invested capital: ROIC is meaningless; use the high-growth case in `references/valuation.md`. Cyclicals: use three to five year averages. High inflation: nominal ROIC rises mechanically (McKinsey ch. 29).
- Not in the sources: the FactSet ROIC definition (tax rate, goodwill, leases, average or year-end capital). Test it against the hand-built figure.
- Not in the sources: a fitted speed of ROIC reversion by sector. The persistence figures are for CFROI; state the r used and that it is a proxy.
- Not in the sources: amortizable R&D lives by industry beyond pharma (about 10 years) and software (short). State the life as an assumption and show one alternative.

# Industry structure and moat

This method decides whether a company's return above its cost of capital is likely to last, by testing the structure of its industry first and the company's own advantage second, in the sequence of Mauboussin and Callahan's "Measuring the Moat" (2013). A moat has two dimensions: magnitude (the spread over the cost of capital times the capital that can earn it) and duration (how long the spread lasts). Advantage needs two tests passed over a full cycle: a return above the cost of capital, and a return above competitors (pp. 3-4). The output is a balance of evidence, an assumed duration in years and what would change it. It is never a moat rating or score.

## When a skill loads this file

Moat, deep dive, thesis, sector and theme work, and any valuation that sets a competitive advantage period or a fade. Load `references/roic.md` with it: the spread and the margin and turnover split come from there. A narrow question ("does the company have pricing power") gets the relevant step with its evidence, not the full sequence.

## Inputs

| Input | Where in Bigdata.com | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| ROIC, margins, revenue, invested capital for the company and each peer | `bigdata_company_tearsheet`, `financial_statements, financial_ratios, key_metrics` | reported |
| Revenue by product and geography, five years | `revenue_segmentation` | reported |
| Peer candidates | `bigdata_screen_companies`, peers named in filings, `mergers_acquisitions` | reported |
| Industry size and shares, supplier and customer concentration, contract terms, price changes, capacity, entrants and exits | `bigdata_search` (one aspect and one period per call; see the evidence table) | reported |
| Hiring by rivals and entrants | `hiring_trends` section, news | reported |
| Cost of capital | Not in Bigdata.com; see `references/roic.md` | assumed |

Not in the sources and not in the tearsheet: industry totals and private-company shares. Take them from filings or research and say when shares cover listed companies only.

## Procedure

1. **Set the unit and the stage.** Analyze the business unit, not the conglomerate, and aggregate (p. 9). Place it in a life-cycle phase: innovation (rising returns, heavy reinvestment), fading (excess but declining), mature (returns near the cost of capital), subpar (below it), with a reason (p. 4). Class the industry: fragmented, emerging, mature, declining, international, network or hypercompetitive (p. 17, after Barney). Done when the unit, phase and class are stated.
2. **Draw the industry map.** Suppliers, customers, complementors, regulators and potential entrants; firms in order of dominance; payment terms and incentives between them; labor and regulation (p. 11). Done when the map table names each party and how it touches profit.
3. **Build the profit pool.** Width = each firm's share of industry invested capital, height = ROIC minus WACC, area = economic profit. Use three to five year averages, for today and five and ten years ago (p. 13; Profit Pools 2016, pp. 1-2). Add the four-firm revenue ratio and the top-ten share of capital. Read it as: is the pool positive on average, who holds the width, are high-spread firms gaining width or only spread, which wide firms destroy value. Done when the table shows who gained or lost width and spread.
4. **Test share stability** (formula below). Done when one number and a verdict are stated.
5. **Test pricing power.** Five-year price trend of the product; split each margin change into price, mix and volume (p. 16; Operating Leverage 2016, pp. 8-10). Stable or rising prices go with a stable, slow-cycle industry, falling prices with a fast-cycle one. Ask whether the industry passed on supplier cost increases. Done when the price evidence is dated and cited.
6. **Test rivalry.** HHI or four-firm ratio; similarity of goals and ownership (public, private, private equity); asset specificity, which keeps firms in; demand variability with high fixed costs, which brings capacity at the peak and price wars in the trough; industry growth, since slow growth makes share gains zero-sum (pp. 25-27). Done when each item has evidence or a gap.
7. **Test entry and exit first among the forces.** Threat of entry is the most important force (pp. 19-25), so test barriers before the rest: where they are low, entry pushes returns toward the cost of capital whatever the other forces show. Use the base rates and the barrier list below. An entrant weighs the incumbent's likely reaction (asset specificity, scale, excess capacity, reputation) and its own payoff (precommitment contracts, patents, learning curve, network effects). Done when barriers are named with evidence and recent entrants and exits are listed.
8. **Run the remaining forces as root-cause tests**, not as an attractiveness label (p. 18):
   - Suppliers: more concentrated than the industry; no substitutes; high switching cost; the industry is a small share of their sales; the input is critical; credible forward integration.
   - Buyers: concentration against sellers; the product's share of the buyer's cost; differentiation; switching cost; information; credible backward integration; price sensitivity of end users.
   - Substitutes: other ways to do the same job, their price and performance, switching cost and how fast they are improving. Substitutes set a ceiling on price.
   Done when each force has a one-line verdict with its evidence.
9. **Map the value chain** by discrete activity (R&D, supply chain, operations, marketing and sales, service) and compare with peers. A chain that looks like the peers' means competition to be the best, and price wars (p. 33). Value created = willingness to pay minus opportunity cost (p. 32). Done when the activities that differ from peers are named.
10. **Identify the source of advantage and test it against the numbers** (pp. 34-41):
    - Production: process (indivisibility, complexity, rate of cost decline, legal protection, unique resources) and scale (distribution, purchasing, R&D, advertising). Signature: lower gross margin, high asset turnover. Scale is mostly local or regional (Total Addressable Market 2015, p. 16).
    - Consumer: habit, experience goods, switching costs and lock-in, network effects. Signature: high gross margin. Switching costs are financial (fees, implementation), procedural (training, data migration, integration) and relational; gather retention, churn and contract length where disclosed.
    - External: subsidies, tariffs, quotas, licenses, regulation.
    - Efficient scale: a market that supports only a few profitable firms at minimum efficient scale; the advantage belongs to whoever holds the position.
    A brand counts only if it raises willingness to pay or lowers supplier cost; two of the ten owners of the top ten brands missed their cost of capital (pp. 46-47). Done when ROIC split into margin and turnover over five to ten years matches the claimed source.
11. **Test interaction and disruption.** Capacity and price behavior of rivals: a repeated game with clear signals is stable, a single-play capacity race is not (pp. 42-45). Classify innovation as sustaining, low-end disruptive or new-market disruptive; ask whether products overshoot customer needs, whether competition is shifting to speed and convenience, and whether components are modularizing (pp. 27-31). Done when one verdict is written.
12. **Conclude on magnitude and duration** with the rules below. Done when the duration in years, its evidence, the fade endpoint and what would change the view are stated.

Evidence to search, one aspect per call:

| Step | Search for | Documents |
|---|---|---|
| 2, 8 | named suppliers, customers, regulators; customer concentration; contract terms | filings (business, risk factors), transcripts |
| 3, 4 | industry size, shares, peer results | research, filings, news |
| 5 | price increases, volume response, discounting, mix | transcripts, news |
| 6, 7 | capacity additions, entrants, exits, deals, price wars | news, transcripts, M&A history |
| 10 | retention, lock-in, scale economics, patents and expiries | filings, transcripts |
| 11 | low-price entrants, new-market products | news, research, job postings |

## Formulas

- Share stability = (1/N) x sum over competitors of |share(t) - share(t-5)|, in percentage points, N = number of competitors (pp. 15-16).
- HHI = 10,000 x sum of squared market shares (as fractions) of the 50 largest firms. Shares of 40, 30, 20 and 10 percent give 3,000 (pp. 25-26).
- Four-firm ratio = revenue share of the four largest firms (Profit Pools, p. 1).
- Economic profit = invested capital x (ROIC - WACC); a $200m capital base at a 5-point spread is $10m (p. 13).
- Learning curve: unit cost falls by a fixed share each time cumulative output doubles; about 20 percent for the median product (pp. 19-25). Project cost from cumulative production, not from time, and state a floor set by input costs (Trancik interview, 2017, pp. 4-5).

{"results":[{"id":"F0D8A94B710916632FADB086B5606949","headline":"ASML Holding N.V.: Q3 2026 Earnings Calls on Oct 14, 2026 - Transcript","timestamp":"2026-10-14T00:00:00","source":{"name":"S&P Global Transcripts"},"chunks":[{"cnum":3,"text":"So then with that strong quarter behind us, how are you looking at Q4 and the full year then for '26?
For Q4, we expect revenue between EUR 14.2 billion and EUR 15.2 billion. So again, a very good step-up, and that is also what we expected, right? We said that we expect the second half to be stronger than the first half. And you see that momentum really very, very strongly building up. So EUR 14.2 billion to EUR 15.2 billion there.
In terms of installed base business, again, we expect an increase there. We expect EUR 3.7 billion installed base business for the quarter, again, largely driven, I would say, by upgrades. A gross margin, we expect around 57% for the quarter. If we translate all of that into what does it mean for the full year? So for the full year '26, we therefore now expect our sales to be between EUR 44 billion and EUR 45 billion for the year, and we expect a gross margin of around 56%.
So what does that mean then for the different parts of the business in 2026?
So against the backdrop of an overall 36% increase for '26 in comparison to '25, you see that, that is largely driven by EUV. So the EUV business grows over 45% this year. We expect the non-EUV business to be around 20% growth for -- in comparison to last year and the installed base business around 50%. The China part of the total business, we expect to be around 20%."},{"cnum":4,"text":"So then maybe just going a bit deeper on the gross margin. I think at the beginning of the year, we had a guide of between 51% and 53%. Certainly, things have gotten stronger since then. Can you share a little bit maybe on the dynamics that have led to that improved outlook?
Absolutely. So what are the key drivers? Of course, volume helps, right? Clearly, we have increased our expectation in terms of total sales and higher volume obviously leads to better fixed cost coverage. So that is a positive for the gross margin. Also, mix is important. If you look at EUV and immersion as key drivers for the gross margin, both of them are pretty strong.
And also, obviously, as I mentioned before, the installed base business and the upgrade business included in there is a very, very strong driver of the gross margin. So as a result of that, indeed, as you say, 56% is the expectation for the full year, which is a very, very nice step-up from the expectations at the beginning of the year.
But I think we also talked last quarter about higher value-based pricing and the contribution that might play on the gross margin. How is that showing up as part of the outlook?
Yes. So we completed those conversations. So that's been done with the key customers. The effect of that is not really visible in '26. It will start to become visible partly in the course of 2027. I think the full impact of that you will start to see in '28 and beyond."}],"url":"https://app.bigdata.com/documents/F0D8A94B710916632FADB086B5606949?cnum=3&cnum=4"},{"id":"DCD3DA8A66FF90AAD5397279C492EF0C","headline":"ASML Holding N.V.: Q3 2026 Earnings Calls on Oct 14, 2026 - Transcript","timestamp":"2026-10-14T13:00:00","source":{"name":"S&P Global Transcripts"},"chunks":[{"cnum":7,"text":"In summary, the third quarter was a record for both total net sales and gross margin, and we expect our business to continue to accelerate in the fourth quarter as we execute against a backdrop of very strong customer demand for all our products and services.
With that, I would like to turn the call back over to Christophe.
If we take a step back to look at the market environment, we see that the pace of the AI build-out continues to be very robust. Supply shortages across advanced Logic and Memory nodes continue to increase in size and in time horizon. Against this backdrop, we had very constructive discussions with our customers throughout the quarter and the demand signals we have received have continued to strengthen."},{"cnum":5,"text":"Turning to the balance sheet. We ended the third quarter with cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments at a level of EUR 12.7 billion. Our free cash flow in Q3 was EUR 11.4 billion, underpinning the strong order momentum of our customers and the related down payments.
Moving to the cash return to our shareholders. In Q3, ASML paid the first interim dividend over 2026 of EUR 1.88 per ordinary share. Further, we purchased in Q3 around EUR 4.1 billion worth of shares under the current 2026-2028 share buyback program. The second quarterly interim dividend over 2026 will be EUR 1.88 per ordinary share and will be made payable on November 4, 2026.
With that, I would like to turn to our expectations for the fourth quarter and the full year 2026. We expect Q4 total net sales to be between EUR 14.2 billion and EUR 15.2 billion with a gross margin of around 57%. We expect our Q4 Installed Base Management sales to be around EUR 3.7 billion. The expected R&D expenses for Q4 are around EUR 1.2 billion and SG&A is expected to be around EUR 0.4 billion."},{"cnum":25,"text":"Quickly, Roger, on the gross margin, your guidance on gross margin in the fourth quarter is down from the current quarter, even though your revenues are going up significantly. And then, I mean, just again, regarding the response you made earlier about the value-based pricing, should we assume that most of the value-based pricing-related increases will go straight down to the gross margin line? Or is there a margin number on the increases that you will be putting through?
So on the first one, the gross margin in Q4, a little bit lower from Q3. That is primarily related to the fact that we are seeing some ramp costs, right? So we're ramping up for the increases that Christophe was just talking about. That has a bit of a bearing on the gross margin expectation. And that's why the fixed cost coverage that you would expect to benefit from the higher volume is a little bit compensated and a bit more compensated by the extra cost that we incur in the ramp as we see it now in Q4. So that's the main reason that we have there."},{"cnum":3,"text":"With that, I would like to turn the call over to Christophe Fouquet for a brief introduction.
Welcome, everyone, and thank you for joining us for our third quarter 2026 results conference call. Before we begin the Q&A session, Roger and I would like to provide an overview and some commentary on the third quarter 2026 results as well as provide some additional comments on the current business environment and on our future business outlook.
Thank you, Christophe, and welcome, everyone. I will first review the third quarter 2026 financial accomplishments and then provide guidance on the fourth quarter and the full year of 2026. Let me start with our third quarter accomplishments. Total net sales in the third quarter of 2026 were a record at EUR 11.7 billion, towards the high end of our guidance and reflecting strong execution of our capacity ramp. Net system sales were EUR 8.4 billion, which includes EUR 4.1 billion from EUV system sales, including the sale of 1 High NA EUV system and EUR 4.3 billion from non-EUV system sales."},{"cnum":15,"text":"And then as a follow-up, you talked about in the prepared remarks or in the transcript, value-based pricing impacting more 2027, 2028. Can you share any just a few more additional details on that, how to think about just kind of the trajectory of gross margin from here?
Yes. So those are 2 questions, right? So first, on the pricing. As we mentioned in July, we -- at that point, we were entering into conversations with customers on price increases. Those conversations have been completed and have indeed led to pricing increase for what we call the most critical products for our customers. So that has been done. We also -- and you made reference to it, as we said in the prepared remarks, this is not going to have an impact on '26. You will see some impact on '27, but I would say that the full impact of that is really going to start in '28. So from '28 onwards, you're going to see a sustained impact of that, but you will see -- in the course of '27, you will see that starting to manifest itself in a positive way in both our revenue and the ASPs and in the gross margin.
Your second question on gross margin is obviously a much broader question, but let me take that one then. So what are the puts and takes on the gross margin? So as you have seen, gross margin this quarter, very, very strong and stronger than we anticipated, I would say, primarily as a result of the EUR 400 million more upgrade business that we have. But we should also not forget that if you look at the total year at 56%, it's not just the upgrade business, right? It's also higher volume. It's also the fact that we had a very strong Low NA EUV business in there, very strong immersion business in there. So those are all things that help."},{"cnum":6,"text":"Regarding our full year expectations, we expect our full year 2026 total net sales to be between EUR 44 billion and EUR 45 billion with a gross margin of around 56%. This anticipated year-over-year total net sales increase of around 36% reflects our expectation of over 45% growth in EUV, around 20% growth in non-EUV-related system sales and around 50% growth in Installed Base Management sales.
Turning to end use. This year, we expect Logic net system sales to grow around 10% and Memory net system sales to grow around 75%. The growth in Memory is driven by the combination of capacity expansion of our customers and the increasing adoption of EUV on advanced DRAM nodes. As previously mentioned, we continue to expect the China region to account for around 20% of our total net sales this year."},{"cnum":16,"text":"And then obviously, the question is how will that develop into the years beyond this year, right? So what's the implication for '27 and beyond. And of course, we're not going to give you a gross margin percentage for '27, that will come in January of 2027. But if you look at the key drivers of the gross margin this year, you have to ask yourself how much of that can be sustained into 2027. So first off, volume with everything that Christophe just told you on the 30% increase in 2027, of course, volume should help, right? And volume, as long as we're able to control the cost of the increase in capacity, volume should give you better fixed cost coverage. So that should be a positive in that regard.
The second element is mix. And there, too, again, key drivers of the volume are the 30% extra in immersion and Low NA EUV. Both of them are obviously very positive from a gross margin perspective. Of course, there will be quite some dry business that we continue to increase this year, but also next year. But I would say that also mix with the strength in EUV demand and immersion demand, that should help. Then to your point, we have the price increase, which, as I mentioned, will have some effect in '27, the larger effect you will see in '28, but it will have some effect in '27. So that's going to be helpful."},{"cnum":4,"text":"Net system sales were split between Logic at 54% and Memory at 46%. Gross margin for the quarter was above guidance at 57.5%, primarily due to the contribution of very high-margin components within our Installed Base Management business. Our operating expenses were as guided with R&D expenses at around EUR 1.2 billion and SG&A expenses at around EUR 0.4 billion. The effective tax rate for Q3 was 16.1%.
