results.headline: ASML Holding (ASML NL) - Even capacity expansion cannot keep up with demand, 'Overweight'

chunks.text:
8. ASML Holding Shareholder Returns and Relative Stock Price Comparison
Valuation burden is not high when reflecting equipment profit growth, but caution is advised regarding volatility
Reflecting ASML's equipment profit growth, the valuation burden has eased to a level similar to its peers. ASML's 12MF P/E is 29.6x, which is higher than the Dutch market at 15.3x and the semiconductor industry at 20.3x. However, the PEG reflecting the 43.0% EPS CAGR for the next 3 years (2026–2028) is 0.7x, which is similar to peers Lam Research (0.7x) and Applied Materials (0.6x).
The drop in multiples compared to last quarter's P/E of 37.7x and PEG of 1.1x is due to the upward revision of EPS estimates (CAGR 33.0% -> 43.0%) outstripping the stock price increase; the high P/E is judged to be a premium supported by earnings growth.
The 12MF P/B is 17.3x, down from 20.6x last quarter, and ROE has improved from 53.7% to 56.9%, somewhat reducing the stock price burden relative to equity. However, EV/EBITDA of 23.2x and EV/Sales of 10.6x still significantly exceed the semiconductor industry averages of 14.7x and 7.8x, respectively, maintaining a qualitative premium.
Within peer companies, processor makers such as NVIDIA (PEG 0.2x) and Broadcom (PEG 0.3x) have lower multiples, limiting the relative valuation attractiveness of equipment makers. While the mid-to-long-term growth story remains valid, it is necessary to watch for increased short-term volatility.

Price increase negotiations completed; effects to be partially reflected in 2027 and fully realized from 2028
Price negotiations that began last quarter have been finalized. The increase targets high-spec bilateral pricing that provides the most value to customers, and upgrade pricing will also be adjusted in the same direction in linkage with long-term pricing. Due to lead times, the effect will not be seen in 2026, will be partially reflected in 2027, and will be fully reflected from 2028. While part of the increase is used for internal ramp-up costs and supply chain support following production increases, a significant portion contributes directly to gross margin. The CFO emphasized that this increase is not planned to be repeated annually, but was conducted within a framework of maintaining value-based pricing principles so as not to be exposed to price reduction pressure when the market slows down.

October 15, 2026
Solid long-term growth expectations based on AI-driven semiconductor shortage; maintain Overweight
ASML Holding (ASML) reaffirmed its long-term guidance and maintained long-term earnings visibility amid the unresolved AI-driven semiconductor shortage. Caution is needed regarding high volatility following short-term surges. We maintain an 'Overweight' opinion as demand outstrips supply and is accompanied by earnings growth. ASML's 12MF P/E is 29.6x, with a PEG of 0.7x reflecting a 43.0% EPS CAGR for the next 3 years (2026–2028). This is similar to LRap Research's 0.7x and AMAT's 0.6x. The 12MF P/B has declined from 20.6x to 17.3x, and ROE has improved to 56.9%, easing the additional burden on capital.

chunks.text:
Credit View
The annual outlook for revenue and gross margin has been raised again, exceeding capital market expectations. Semiconductor manufacturers are increasing demand for machines, which ASML cannot fully meet despite the already announced capacity increase of +30% for 2027. As a result, the Group is considering increasing capacities in 2028 beyond the previously considered +30%. At the same time, the Group is adjusting its pricing strategy, with positive effects on results starting from 2027 and particularly from 2028. For revenue, ASML now expects EUR 44 to 45 billion for 2026 (previously: EUR 43 to 45 billion). Profitability is also expected to be more optimistic. The gross margin is expected to rise from 52.8% in 2026 to historically high levels of around 56% (previously: 54% to 56%). With this, ASML would have already reached the lower end of the profitability targeted for 2030 of 56% to 60%. The targeted range of EUR 44 to 60 billion for revenue by 2030 could also be exceeded by 2028 at the latest. Profitability, balance sheet ratios, and credit metrics should continue to remain at a robust level. However, due to the significant spread tightening that has already occurred, the outstanding bonds do not appear attractive to us.

122-## How the sector makes money and the value drivers
123-
--
127:- **Price declines and the learning curve.** Prices for a given level of performance fall every year. Measuring the Moat (2013) shows semiconductor prices falling about 8.6 percent a year in 2006-2011, the steepest of the fast-cycle examples quoted (verify). Profit depends on moving down the cost curve faster than price: the median product cuts unit cost about 20 percent for each doubling of cumulative output.
128-- **Utilization.** With most costs fixed, gross margin follows fab or factory loading. Changes in capacity utilization correlate about 0.60 with changes in operating margin across large companies (1967-2015).
129-- **Capital intensity and reinvestment.** Leading-edge capacity and tools are expensive and arrive in large blocks; fabless designers carry R&D but little fixed capital.
130-- **Product cycles and design wins.** A win in a customer's platform sets revenue for its life; a missed node or generation is hard to recover.
--
160:- **Cyclical returns.** McKinsey lists semiconductors among cyclical industries, with chemicals, oil and gas and metals (ch.4, median ROIC 1965-2007, verify). Supply drives the cycle: capacity is added when returns are high and arrives in large blocks, and utilization and returns fall about two years later (the commodity chemicals pattern, McKinsey ch.35). Memory is the clearest case.
161-- **Capacity races.** Each firm gains from adding capacity alone; when all add, the payoff is lowest (a prisoner's dilemma, Measuring the Moat). Watch announced capex across the whole industry, not one firm.
162-- **S-curve overshoot.** Color TV makers built 14 million units of capacity against peak sales of 6 million because they extrapolated mid-curve growth (TAM 2015). Apply the same check to any new end market.
163-- **Replacement cycles.** Once replacements dominate unit demand (within 5 to 12 years for most products), forecast the replacement cycle, not penetration. A one-year lengthening of the cycle cut cumulative 15-year units 17 percent in the paper's example. In 2015 PCs were in the replacement stage and smartphones in transition (verify current stages).
--
165:- **Concentration** (HOLT profit pools, data June 2016, verify): computers and peripherals, 275 firms, four-firm ratio 42.4 percent, top ten's share of invested capital 64 / 60 / 72 percent (2005 / 2010 / 2015); communications equipment, 366 firms, 48.2 percent, 67 / 68 / 64. Semiconductors were not broken out in the notes.
166-- **Sources of advantage.** Production advantages (process know-how, scale in fabs and tools, learning curve) show as lower gross margin and high asset turnover; design and ecosystem advantages (software stacks, standards, switching costs for developers) show as high gross margin (Measuring the Moat, pp.34-41).
167-- **Modularization.** When components standardize, the industry shifts from integrated to horizontal and value moves to the bottleneck layer (computers 1980 against 1995).

Listed REITs compete for assets with private real estate funds, pension funds and sovereign investors, and private buyers often set the marginal cap rate (judgment, verify). Advantages come from location quality that new supply cannot replicate, scale in operating platforms (apartments, self-storage, logistics), tenant relationships, and a lower cost of capital that lets a REIT buy accretively. 127:- **Price declines and the learning curve.** Prices for a given level of performance fall every year. Measuring the Moat (2013) shows semiconductor prices falling about 8.6 percent a year in 2006-2011, the steepest of the fast-cycle examples quoted (verify). Profit depends on moving down the cost curve faster than price: the median product cuts unit cost about 20 percent for each doubling of cumulative output.
128-- **Utilization.** With most costs fixed, gross margin follows fab or factory loading. Changes in capacity utilization correlate about 0.60 with changes in operating margin across large companies (1967-2015).
129-- **Capital intensity and reinvestment.** Leading-edge capacity and tools are expensive and arrive in large blocks; fabless designers carry R&D but little fixed capital.
130-- **Product cycles and design wins.** A win in a customer's platform sets revenue for its life; a missed node or generation is hard to recover.
--
160:- **Cyclical returns.** McKinsey lists semiconductors among cyclical industries, with chemicals, oil and gas and metals (ch.4, median ROIC 1965-2007, verify). Supply drives the cycle: capacity is added when returns are high and arrives in large blocks, and utilization and returns fall about two years later (the commodity chemicals pattern, McKinsey ch.35). Memory is the clearest case.
161-- **Capacity races.** Each firm gains from adding capacity alone; when all add, the payoff is lowest (a prisoner's dilemma, Measuring the Moat). Watch announced capex across the whole industry, not one firm.
162-- **S-curve overshoot.** Color TV makers built 14 million units of capacity against peak sales of 6 million because they extrapolated mid-curve growth (TAM 2015). Apply the same check to any new end market.
163-- **Replacement cycles.** Once replacements dominate unit demand (within 5 to 12 years for most products), forecast the replacement cycle, not penetration. A one-year lengthening of the cycle cut cumulative 15-year units 17 percent in the paper's example. In 2015 PCs were in the replacement stage and smartphones in transition (verify current stages).
--
165:- **Concentration** (HOLT profit pools, data June 2016, verify): computers and peripherals, 275 firms, four-firm ratio 42.4 percent, top ten's share of invested capital 64 / 60 / 72 percent (2005 / 2010 / 2015); communications equipment, 366 firms, 48.2 percent, 67 / 68 / 64. Semiconductors were not broken out in the notes.
166-- **Sources of advantage.** Production advantages (process know-how, scale in fabs and tools, learning curve) show as lower gross margin and high asset turnover; design and ecosystem advantages (software stacks, standards, switching costs for developers) show as high gross margin (Measuring the Moat, pp.34-41).
167-- **Modularization.** When components standardize, the industry shifts from integrated to horizontal and value moves to the bottleneck layer (computers 1980 against 1995).
168-
--
171:Historical base rates, not current facts (verify against current data). Semiconductors and hardware are pooled with software under "Information technology"; sub-industry rates are not in the sources.
172-
173-| Measure | Information technology | Comparison | Sample |
174-|---|---|---|---|
--
187:- **Consensus ignores the cycle.** Forecasts for cyclicals trend upward through peaks and troughs, so a forward P/E looks cheap at the peak and expensive at the trough. Market prices behaved like a 50/50 blend of perfect and zero foresight in McKinsey's sample (1985-1997, verify).
188-- **EV/EBITDA across business models is invalid.** Higher capital intensity gives a lower EV/EBITDA; compare foundries and memory with each other, and use EV/EBIT or EV/NOPAT when fabless and manufacturing peers are mixed (multiples notes 2.4).
189-- **P/B and EV/invested capital** for memory and capital-heavy names, read next to ROIC (EV/IC = EV/NOPLAT x ROIC).
190-- **High growth** in a new end market (AI accelerators, judgment): treat with the high-growth method (steady state 10 to 15 years out, addressable market at acceptable returns, scenarios), and test the S-curve and capacity against demand.
--
223:- Fees and commissions: advisory, underwriting, asset management, payments, brokerage. About half of net revenue for investment banks in the same text (verify). Underwriting and advisory fees are cyclical.
224-- Trading income: volatile; several years of gains can be lost in one year.
225-
226-Value depends on return on equity (ROE) against the cost of equity, growth of the equity base, and the capital ratio regulators and depositors require (McKinsey ch. 36, p. 782). Leverage magnifies everything: in McKinsey's ABC Bank example (equity 8% of assets), a one-point change in the loan rate moved ROE by about 12 points (p. 780). Funding rests on confidence that "can disappear overnight" (p. 766). For these reasons, value a bank with scenarios, not a point estimate.
--
261:Banks compete on a low-cost, stable deposit base, scale in technology and payments, underwriting discipline and regulatory capital as a barrier; nonbank lenders and private credit compete for loans (judgment, verify). Regulation limits capital allocation choices: understand the capital rules before judging buybacks or growth (Mauboussin, Capital Allocation, 2015, p. 45). European banks shifted from interest income toward fees and trading between 1988 and 2007, which made ROE and price to book more cyclical (McKinsey Ex. 36.1-36.2).
262-
263-## Persistence and fade
264-
--
525:Rents are set locally by supply and demand for each property type. New supply arrives with a lag of years, which makes property markets cyclical (judgment). Listed REITs compete for assets with private real estate funds, pension funds and sovereign investors, and private buyers often set the marginal cap rate (judgment, verify). Advantages come from location quality that new supply cannot replicate, scale in operating platforms (apartments, self-storage, logistics), tenant relationships, and a lower cost of capital that lets a REIT buy accretively. Structural demand shifts are large: online retail for logistics and against some shopping centres, remote work for offices, and data and power demand for data centres (judgment, verify current direction). ETFs owned 10.6% of large-cap real estate market value, against 7.8% for utilities and 4.3% for technology (Mauboussin, Looking for Easy Games, 2017, p. 14, data at 30 September 2016; verify), which affects flows and correlation.
526-
527-## Persistence and fade
528-
--
566:Capital goods (aerospace and defense, machinery, electrical equipment, building products, construction and engineering), transportation (rail, trucking, air freight, airlines, marine) and commercial and professional services. Most of the sector is cyclical: sales follow capital spending, construction, freight volumes and government budgets. Services, defense and aftermarket-heavy businesses are the exceptions.
567-
568-## How the sector makes money
569-
--
571:- The installed base generates aftermarket revenue (parts, service, upgrades) that is less cyclical and usually carries a higher margin than original equipment; a margin gap of roughly 15 to 30 points is a judgment range (verify against segment disclosure).
572-- Transport earns on volume times yield over a largely fixed network; incremental margins are high when volume returns to a network built for it.
573-- Value drivers: volume through the cycle, price and mix, aftermarket share of sales, operating leverage on a fixed plant, working capital intensity, and capital intensity. Median real sales growth of industrials correlated about 0.74 with US real GDP growth (top 1,000 global companies, 1950-2014; Mauboussin, Operating Leverage, 2016) (verify), so a macro view is a reasonable starting point for the top line, unlike energy or staples.

--
607:The reason: with perfect foresight, DCF values of cyclicals are nearly flat while cash flows swing widely, and consensus EPS for cyclicals has historically trended upward through peaks and troughs (36 US cyclicals, 1985-1997; McKinsey ch. 35) (verify). A forward P/E at the peak looks cheap and at the trough looks expensive.

# Three-case DCF, EUR bn; valuation at end-2026 discounted ~0.2y back is ignored (approximation)
SH=0.383; NETCASH=10.8; MISTRAL=1.8; TAX=0.17
def run(sales, margins, wacc, g_term, ronic_term, ic_per_sales=0.25, s2026=44.5):
    pv=0; prev=s2026; rows=[]
    for t,(s,m) in enumerate(zip(sales,margins),start=1):
        nopat=s*m*(1-TAX); reinv=ic_per_sales*(s-prev); fcf=nopat-reinv
        pv+=fcf/(1+wacc)**t; prev=s; rows.append((s,m,nopat,fcf))
    n_next=sales[-1]*(1+g_term)*margins[-1]*(1-TAX)
    cv=n_next*(1-g_term/ronic_term)/(wacc-g_term)
    pvcv=cv/(1+wacc)**len(sales)
    ev=pv+pvcv; eq=ev+NETCASH+MISTRAL
    return dict(ev=ev, ps=eq/SH, tv_share=pvcv/ev, cv=cv, impl_mult=cv/(sales[-1]*margins[-1]*(1-TAX)), impl_ev_ebit=cv/(sales[-1]*margins[-1]), rows=rows, pv=pv, pvcv=pvcv)
# 2027..2036 (10 years)
cases={
 'base': ([58.0,68.0,73.0,70.0,75.0,80.0,84.0,87.5,90.5,93.0],[0.44,0.46,0.46,0.43,0.44,0.44,0.43,0.42,0.42,0.42]),
 'bear': ([55.0,46.0,48.0,54.0,58.0,61.0,63.5,65.5,67.5,69.5],[0.42,0.34,0.36,0.39,0.40,0.40,0.39,0.38,0.38,0.38]),
 'bull': ([60.0,74.0,86.0,92.0,99.0,106.0,112.0,117.0,121.0,125.0],[0.45,0.48,0.49,0.48,0.48,0.47,0.47,0.46,0.46,0.46]),
}
res={}
for k,(s,m) in cases.items():
    r=run(s,m,0.09,0.03,0.09); res[k]=r
    cagr=(s[-1]/44.5)**(1/10)-1
    print(k, f"EV {r['ev']:.0f}  per share EUR {r['ps']:.0f}  TV share {r['tv_share']:.0%}  implied terminal EV/NOPAT {r['impl_mult']:.1f} EV/EBIT {r['impl_ev_ebit']:.1f}  10y sales CAGR {cagr:.1%} 2036 sales {s[-1]}")
p={'bear':0.30,'base':0.50,'bull':0.20}
ev=sum(p[k]*res[k]['ps'] for k in p); print("Expected value per share EUR", round(ev))
# also RONIC 20% variant for base
r=run(*cases['base'],0.09,0.03,0.20); print("base w/ terminal RONIC 20%:", round(r['ps']))
# bridge base
b=res['base']; print("bridge base: PV explicit",round(b['pv'],1),"PV CV",round(b['pvcv'],1),"EV",round(b['ev'],1),"+net cash",NETCASH,"+Mistral",MISTRAL,"= equity",round(b['ev']+NETCASH+MISTRAL,1),"/ shares bn",SH)
print("WACC x g (base, per share EUR):")
for w in [0.08,0.085,0.09,0.095,0.10]:
    print(w, [round(run(*cases['base'],w,g,w)['ps']) for g in [0.02,0.025,0.03,0.035]])
# market-implied: steady state
price_eur=1589.6/1.08; mcap=price_eur*SH; ev_mkt=mcap-NETCASH-MISTRAL
nop27=25.9*(1-TAX)
print("price EUR",round(price_eur),"mcap",round(mcap),"EV",round(ev_mkt),"NOPAT27",round(nop27,1),"steady-state EV",round(nop27/0.09,1),"share of EV from future value creation",f"{1-nop27/0.09/ev_mkt:.0%}")
print("PE27", price_eur/58.4, "PE26 ex Mistral", price_eur/(42.3-1.3), "EV/EBIT27", ev_mkt/25.9)
# implied CAP: years of growth at g with RONIC=30%? solve years of constant 12% NOPAT growth then steady state with RONIC 40% reinvestment
def implied(years, g, ronic=0.40, wacc=0.09):
    n=nop27; pv=0
    for t in range(1,years+1):
        fcf=n*(1-g/ronic); pv+=fcf/(1+wacc)**t; n*=1+g
    pv+= (n/wacc)/(1+wacc)**years
    return pv
for g in [0.08,0.10,0.12,0.15]:
    for y in range(1,30):
        if implied(y,g)>=ev_mkt: print(f"implied CAP at NOPAT growth {g:.0%}: {y} years"); break
    else: print(g,"not reached in 30y")
# warranted P/E for value driver: P/E = (1-g/RONIC)/(WACC-g) on NOPAT
for g,ro in [(0.03,0.09),(0.03,0.20),(0.04,0.30)]:
    print("warranted EV/NOPAT g",g,"RONIC",ro, round((1-g/ro)/(0.09-g),1))
print("actual EV/NOPAT27", round(ev_mkt/nop27,1))

for g,ro in [(0.03,0.09),(0.03,0.20),(0.04,0.30)]:
    print("warranted EV/NOPAT g",g,"RONIC",ro, round((1-g/ro)/(0.09-g),1))
print("actual EV/NOPAT27", round(ev_mkt/nop27,1))

content.text:
# ASML Holding (ASML): deep dive, 23 October 2026

Data as of: price 22 Oct 2026 (Nasdaq close $1,589.60); consensus estimates retrieved 23 Oct 2026 (FactSet, quarterly records); statements FY2021 to FY2025 annual and Q3 2026 quarterly; newest document 23 Oct 2026.

## What the evidence shows

ASML is the only supplier of EUV lithography tools, the machines needed for the most advanced logic and DRAM chips. It also sells DUV (deep ultraviolet) scanners, metrology tools, and service and upgrades to a growing installed base. 2026 sales are guided to €44-45bn with a gross margin of about 56% [1]. That is 36% growth, and it already reaches the bottom of the 2030 targets the company set in 2024 (€44-60bn sales, 56-60% gross margin) [2].

The economics are very strong and partly financed by customers. Prepayments (contract liabilities) of €16.0bn at end-2025 exceed the company's operating capital excluding goodwill. ROIC before that customer funding was 42% in 2025 (derived). Reported earnings are mostly clean. The exceptions are a €0.5bn revaluation gain on the Mistral AI stake in Q3 2026 net income [1], and a margin mix that leans on high-margin installed-base upgrades.

Over 2021-2025, management returned €31.9bn through buybacks and dividends, about 109% of FactSet free cash flow, and cut the average share count by about 6.5%. The one non-core deal is €1.3bn for 11% of Mistral AI [3].

At about €1,472 per share (derived), the price matches the consensus path: about €73bn of sales in 2028, then steady growth at a 45% operating margin and no cyclical downturn for 15 years, discounted at 8.5-9%. My three cases give €702 to €1,514 per share, with a probability-weighted value of about €1,082 (derived). That is roughly a quarter below the current price.

The main risk is the semiconductor equipment cycle, with China export rules second. The next dated test is the Q4 2026 report with 2027 guidance in late January 2027.

## The business

ASML sells three things:
- **EUV systems**: Low-NA tools at roughly $200m and High-NA tools at roughly $400m [4].
- **Non-EUV systems**: DUV immersion and dry scanners, plus metrology and inspection.
- **Installed Base Management**: service, upgrades and spare parts. This part is growing fastest because customers buy throughput upgrades to get capacity before new fabs are ready [1].

**2026 mix and units**

| Item | 2026 figure | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total net sales guide | €44-45bn, about +36% | reported | [1] |
| EUV sales growth | over +45% | reported | [1] |
| Non-EUV system sales growth | about +20% | reported | [1] |
| Installed Base sales growth | about +50% | reported | [1] |
| Logic / Memory system sales growth | about +10% / about +75% | reported | [1] |
| Q3 2026 system sales: EUV / non-EUV | €4.1bn / €4.3bn; Logic 54%, Memory 46% | reported | [1] |
| Low-NA EUV units | 44 (2025), about 65 (2026), +30% capacity in 2027, more than +30% under study for 2028 | reported | [1] |
| China share of sales | about 20% (2026 guide); about 16% in H1 2026 | reported | [1], [5] |

**Geography (customer location)**

| Region | 2024 | 2025 | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| China | 36.1% | 29.1% | reported | [6] |
| Taiwan | 15.4% | 25.5% | reported | [7] |
| South Korea | 22.7% | 25.0% | reported | [7] |

**Five-year trend (FactSet, EUR bn)**

| | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 18.61 | 21.17 | 27.56 | 28.26 | 32.67 | reported | Data |
| Gross margin | 51.9% | 49.5% | 50.2% | 49.8% | 51.6% | derived | Data |
| EBIT margin | 35.1% | 30.7% | 32.8% | 31.9% | 34.6% | derived | Data |
| Net income | 5.88 | 5.62 | 7.84 | 7.57 | 9.61 | reported | Data |
| Free cash flow (FactSet definition) | 8.58 | 4.65 | 0.94 | 6.65 | 8.53 | reported | Data |
| EPS (€) | 14.36 | 14.14 | 19.91 | 19.25 | 24.73 | reported | Data |

FactSet's gross margin for 2025 (51.6%) is below the company's 52.8% [8] because FactSet classifies costs differently.

Over five years, profit has moved toward EUV and the installed base. The company's 2026 outlook attributes the margin rise to EUV volume, immersion volume and upgrades [1]. The tearsheet's segment table was empty, so a five-year segment-margin series is not available (see Gaps).

## Economics

ROIC is shown on two bases. The FactSet field is given separately and not mixed into the table.

| Year | Tax rate | NOPAT (€bn) | Operating capital incl. goodwill (€bn) | ROIC on it | Capital before customer prepayments (€bn) | ROIC on it | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 15.2% | 5.54 | 6.25 | 88.7%* | 14.18 | 39.1%* | derived |
| 2022 | 15.0% | 5.52 | 4.92 | 98.9% | 17.40 | 35.0% | derived |
| 2023 | 15.8% | 7.61 | 9.80 | 103.4% | 21.24 | 39.4% | derived |
| 2024 | 18.6% | 7.35 | 8.42 | 80.6% | 20.99 | 34.8% | derived |
| 2025 | 17.7% | 9.31 | 7.37 | 117.9% | 23.37 | 42.0% | derived |

*2021 uses end-year capital only, because the 2020 balance sheet is not in the data.

How the table is built:
- NOPAT is EBIT times (1 minus the effective tax rate).
- Operating capital is total assets minus cash, short-term investments and long-term investments, minus non-debt current liabilities and other non-current liabilities.
- "Before customer prepayments" adds back contract liabilities (€16.0bn in 2025).
- Returns use average capital.
- Excluding goodwill and intangibles, operating capital is negative in every year. Customers fund the working capital.

**Which ROIC this report quotes.** I quote the 42.0% figure (2025, capital before customer prepayments), because prepayments can reverse in a downturn. The FactSet ROIC field is 47.4% for FY2025 and 66.6% trailing at Q3 2026. It divides by debt plus equity (€24.3bn), which includes about €13bn of cash and leaves out the prepayments.

**Decomposition and incremental returns** (2025, prepayment-adjusted basis):
- ROIC of 42.0% = NOPAT margin 28.5% × capital turnover 1.47.
- Return on incremental capital: 41% for 2021→2025 and 63% for 2022→2025.
- Spread over an assumed 9% cost of capital: about 33 points.

## Industry structure and moat

| Item | Evidence | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market position | Only producer of EUV tools. China is barred from EUV and some advanced DUV. | reported | [5] |
| Cost to enter | EUV took more than €6bn of R&D and over 17 years, and depends on Zeiss optics and imec research. | reported | [9] |
| Pricing power | Price increases on the most critical products were agreed with key customers. Some effect in 2027, full effect from 2028. About +10% on service parts to Korea. | reported | [1], [10] |
| Demand visibility | Customers see demand above their supply until at least 2028. Orders are arriving for 2028, and some customers want to order for 2029-2030. Orders come with significant prepayments. | reported | [11], [12] |
| Customer concentration | Largest customer 16.6% of 2024 sales (31.8% in 2023). Top two 30.5% in 2024. | reported | [13] |
| Supplier power | Single-source critical suppliers, including Zeiss for optics. ASML holds a minority stake in Carl Zeiss SMT ($1.11bn, 2016). | reported | [13], Data |
| China substitution | Shanghai Aishengna has started producing immersion DUV tools. SMEE plans 12 DUV tools by end-2026. JPMorgan says a handful of tools is not high-volume manufacturing. | reported | [5], [14] |
| Long-run challenge | Huawei/SiCarrier EUV light-source prototype at about 100-150W against ASML's 250W+. No working chip produced. | reported | [15] |
| Technology roadmap | High-NA in production at Intel. Samsung and SK Hynix plan production use in 2028, TSMC from 2030. Hyper-NA about 10 years out. Larger-mask production readiness by 2033. | reported | [4], [16], [17] |
| Competition in DUV (Nikon, Canon shares) | Not retrieved | gap | n/a |
| Duration of the advantage | EUV leadership through the early 2030s is supported by the High-NA and Hyper-NA roadmap. In DUV, the China share is the most exposed, from 2027-2030. | judgment | n/a |

Base rates set the bounds on persistence. In information technology, operating margins have a 5-year persistence correlation of 0.62 and CFROI (cash flow return on investment) a 4-year correlation of 0.50. Both are among the fastest-fading sectors (top 1,000 global companies 1950-2015, and HOLT global sample 1983-2015; not current facts).

ASML's EUV position is an outlier within that class. I therefore use a 15-year competitive advantage period (judgment), not the sector default.

## Earnings quality

| Measure | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accruals: (net income minus operating cash flow) / average assets | -16.4% | -8.6% | +6.3% | -8.1% | -6.2% | derived |
| FactSet FCF / net income | 1.46 | 0.83 | 0.12 | 0.88 | 0.89 | derived |
| Change in contract liabilities (€bn) | n/a | +4.55 | -1.04 | +1.13 | +3.44 | derived |
| Stock compensation / EBIT | 1.8% | 1.1% | 1.5% | 1.9% | 1.8% | derived |
| Capex / D&A | 2.0 | 2.3 | 3.0 | 2.3 | 1.6 | derived |

**Operating profit rebuild (EBITA, € bn)**

| Item | FY2025 | Trailing 12 months to Q3 2026 | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reported EBIT | 11.30 | 15.21 | reported / derived from quarterly margins |
| + Amortization of acquired intangibles | 0.12 | about 0.12 | reported |
| + Q2 2026 IT transformation charge (once in five years) | 0 | about 0.1 (R&D €1.3bn against about €1.2bn run-rate) | derived [18] |
| Rebuilt EBITA | 11.42 | about 15.4 | derived |
| Below EBIT: Mistral AI revaluation gain (once in five years) | 0 | about 0.5 | reported [1] |

**Flags**

| Flag | Severity | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q3 2026 net income includes about €0.5bn Mistral revaluation (about €1.3 per share) | Low (disclosed) | reported | [1], [19] |
| Margin outperformance came from about €0.4bn of extra high-margin upgrades in Q3 2026. Mirae calls the operating improvement "limited". | Medium | reported | [1], [19] |
| Cash flow follows customer prepayments: Q3 2026 FCF was €11.4bn, 2023 FCF was €0.94bn | Medium (timing) | reported | [1], Data |
| Inventory rose 115% (2021-2025) against revenue +76%. Cash conversion cycle 292 days at FY2025. | Medium (ramp) | derived | Data |
| Goodwill €4.59bn unchanged 2023-2025, no impairment | Low | reported | Data |

Piotroski F-score is 9 (Q3 2026) and Altman Z is 14.6 (Q2 2026), both as reported by FactSet.

## Capital allocation

**Sources and uses, 2021-2025 cumulative (€bn)**

| Item | Amount | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Operating cash flow | 48.6 | reported |
| Capex | -8.2 | reported |
| Buybacks | -20.7 | reported |
| Dividends | -11.3 | reported |
| Mistral AI stake (2025) | -1.3 | reported [3] |
| Net debt change | -0.1 | reported |
| Increase in cash and short-term investments | +5.7 | reported |

**Buybacks.** For 2022-2025, €12.1bn of buybacks reduced the average share count by 21.3m net of issuance (397.7m in 2022 to 388.5m in 2025, from 409.8m in 2021). That implies about €568 per share retired (derived; weighted share counts lag, so this is approximate). Against today's €1,472, that is 2.6 times, or about 33% a year from mid-2023, before dividends. That is well above an assumed 9% cost of equity.

The 2021 programme (€8.6bn) is excluded because the 2020 share count is not in the data. A new programme of up to €12bn runs to end-2028 [8], and €4.1bn was bought in Q3 2026 alone [1].

**Dividend.** €7.50 for 2025, up 17% [8]. Quarterly interims of €1.88 in 2026 [1].

**Deals**

| Deal | Year | Value | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Carl Zeiss SMT minority stake | 2016 | $1.11bn | reported | Data |
| Mapper Lithography | 2019 | undisclosed | reported | Data |
| Berliner Glas (parts) | 2020-21 | $348m disclosed | reported | Data |
| Mistral AI, about 11% stake | 2025 | €1.3bn; revalued up about €0.5bn in Q3 2026 | reported | [3], [1] |

No synergy targets were disclosed, so a premium-versus-synergy test is not possible.

**Leverage.** Net cash of about €10.8bn (derived from the FactSet net debt/EBITDA ratio of -0.66). Debt/EBITDA is 0.12. Rating medians are not in the data.

**Management pay.** The 2026-2028 long-term incentive (LTI) plan weights:
- relative TSR against the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index: 25%
- ROAIC (return on average invested capital): 35%, with threshold 45%, target 55%, stretch 65%
- Technology Leadership Index: 20%
- ESG measures: 20%

These targets were set when the 2026 guide was €34-39bn. ROAIC subtracts current liabilities and non-current contract liabilities from capital, so customer prepayments raise it. FactSet's ROIC field is already 66.6% (a different definition, so it does not settle whether the ROAIC stretch is met). The 2023-2025 plan vested at 137.4% of target [20].

## What the price implies

Assumptions: 9% cost of capital (assumed: euro equity with beta above 1), 17% tax rate (company guide [1]), 383m shares (derived from Q3 2026 net income/EPS), net cash €10.8bn plus Mistral stake about €1.8bn.

- **Steady state.** 2027 consensus EBIT is €25.9bn (sum of quarterly means). After tax that is €21.5bn of NOPAT, worth €239bn at 9% with no growth, or about €652 per share. That is 43% of enterprise value (about €551bn). The other 57% is paid for future value creation.
- **Implied growth and duration.** The price requires about 13 years of 12% annual NOPAT growth after 2027 at a 40% return on new capital, or 10 years at 15% (derived).
- **Warranted multiple compared with actual.** A warranted EV/NOPAT of 14.2x (3% growth, 20% return on new capital) to 17.3x (4%, 30%) compares with an actual 25.6x on 2027 NOPAT. P/E is 25.2x on 2027 consensus EPS of €58.4, and 35.9x on 2026 EPS excluding the Mistral gain.
- **Base rate.** Consensus implies 2025-2028 sales growth of about 30% a year (€32.7bn to about €73bn, with 2028 annualized from three quarters). Among companies with more than $25bn of sales, 4.6% achieved 3-year real growth of 20% or more, and 37.0% had negative 3-year real growth (top 1,000 global companies, 1950-2015, inflation-adjusted; not a current fact). 2026's 36% is already largely in hand. 2027 and 2028 are the part that stands against the base rate.

## Valuation

**Forecast and cases (15 explicit years, 2027-2041; 25% of incremental sales reinvested; 3% terminal growth; 20% terminal return on new capital, judgment)**

| Case | Path | Value per share | Probability | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bear | 2027 €55bn, then a memory/AI capex correction with 2028 sales of €46bn at a 34% EBIT margin. China DUV share lost. 38% mid-cycle margin. | €702 | 25% | assumed |
| Base | 2027 €58bn, 2028 €68bn at 46% margin (pricing). One mid-cycle dip around 2030. Then 5% growth at 42%. | €1,056 | 50% | assumed |
| Bull | Consensus-plus, no downturn: €74bn in 2028, €92bn in 2030, 46-49% margin | €1,514 | 25% | assumed |
| Probability-weighted value | | about €1,082 | | derived |

The weights are judgment. Order coverage for 2027, backed by prepayments [12], argues against a 2027 collapse. The base rate above and the 2023-2024 flat year in the statements argue against assuming no downturn.

**Equity bridge, base case (€bn):** present value of explicit cash flows 226.1 + present value of continuing value 165.8 = enterprise value 391.8; + net cash 10.8 + Mistral stake 1.8 = equity 404.4; divided by 0.383bn shares = €1,056.

**Terminal checks.** Continuing value is 42% of enterprise value. The implied terminal EV/EBIT is 12.1x. Setting the terminal return on new capital equal to the cost of capital lowers the base case to €963.

**Base case per share: cost of capital (rows) × terminal growth (columns)**

| | 2.0% | 2.5% | 3.0% | 3.5% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.0% | 1,185 | 1,220 | 1,261 | 1,310 |
| 8.5% | 1,092 | 1,118 | 1,149 | 1,186 |
| 9.0% | 1,012 | 1,032 | 1,056 | 1,084 |
| 9.5% | 943 | 959 | 977 | 998 |
| 10.0% | 883 | 895 | 909 | 926 |

The consensus path (2027 €58.5bn, 2028 €73bn, then 8% and later 5% growth at a 45% margin) is worth €1,372 at 9% and €1,654 at 8%. The current price sits between the two.

**Comparable companies (trailing multiples at each company's latest period-end price; dates differ)**

| Company | Period end | P/E | EV/EBIT | Gross margin | Op. margin | FactSet ROIC | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ASML | 30 Sep 2026 | 43.5 | 37.7 | 57.4% | 44.4% | 66.6% | reported | Data |
| Applied Materials | 31 Jul 2026 | 46.2 | 44.5 | 50.3% | 33.7% | 32.4% | reported | Data |
| Lam Research | 30 Sep 2026 | 46.9 | 40.6 | 52.3% | 40.0% | 59.7% | reported | Data |
| KLA | 30 Jun 2026 | 82.3 | 70.3 | 62.0% | 43.4% | 48.6% | reported | Data |
| Tokyo Electron | 30 Jun 2026 | 56.8 | 50.4 | 46.8% | 28.9% | 33.6% | reported | Data |

ASML has the lowest trailing EV/EBIT in the group and the highest operating margin. KB Securities puts ASML's forward PEG at 0.7x, against 0.7x for Lam and 0.6x for Applied [19]. Rothschild & Co Redburn shows ASML's forward EV/EBIT premium over peers moving to a discount in 2024 [21].

The comparison does not suggest ASML is expensive relative to peers. The whole group is priced for the AI capex cycle to continue.

**Range:** €702-1,514 per share, with a probability-weighted value of about €1,082, against a current price of about €1,472 (derived).

## Risks and kill criteria

| Rank | Risk | Probability / size | Early signal | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Equipment cycle: AI or memory capex slows after the 2026-2028 build | Medium / large: bear case €702 | Customer capex cuts; memory prices; contract liabilities falling quarter on quarter | judgment | [22], [23] |
| 2 | US MATCH Act bars DUV sales and servicing in China | Medium / about 15-20% of sales plus high-margin service | Bill progress; Dutch alignment | reported | [24], [25] |
| 3 | Ramp execution: supply chain (Zeiss) and ramp costs reduce margins | Medium / medium | Q4 2026 gross margin guided down to about 57% from 57.5% on ramp costs | reported | [1] |

## What the evidence shows

ASML is the only supplier of EUV lithography tools, the machines needed for the most advanced logic and DRAM chips. It also sells DUV (deep ultraviolet) scanners, metrology tools, and service and upgrades to a growing installed base. 2026 sales are guided to €44-45bn with a gross margin of about 56% [1]. That is 36% growth, and it already reaches the bottom of the 2030 targets the company set in 2024 (€44-60bn sales, 56-60% gross margin) [2].

The economics are very strong and partly financed by customers. Prepayments (contract liabilities) of €16.0bn at end-2025 exceed the company's operating capital excluding goodwill. ROIC before that customer funding was 42% in 2025 (derived). Reported earnings are mostly clean. The exceptions are a €0.5bn revaluation gain on the Mistral AI stake in Q3 2026 net income [1], and a margin mix that leans on high-margin installed-base upgrades.

Over 2021-2025, management returned €31.9bn through buybacks and dividends, about 109% of FactSet free cash flow, and cut the average share count by about 6.5%. The one non-core deal is €1.3bn for 11% of Mistral AI [3].

At about €1,472 per share (derived), the price matches the consensus path: about €73bn of sales in 2028, then steady growth at a 45% operating margin and no cyclical downturn for 15 years, discounted at 8.5-9%. My three cases give €702 to €1,514 per share, with a probability-weighted value of about €1,082 (derived). That is roughly a quarter below the current price.

The main risk is the semiconductor equipment cycle, with China export rules second. The next dated test is the Q4 2026 report with 2027 guidance in late January 2027.

2. Contract liabilities fall for two consecutive quarters during 2027.
3. MATCH Act enacted with servicing restrictions.

## What would change this view

1. The 2027 guide (late January 2027) at or above €60bn with a gross margin of 58% or more would move the base case toward the consensus path (€1,372 at 9%).
2. ASML disclosing 2028 order coverage above the 110-unit capacity scenario [12] would lower the bear-case weight.
3. Contract liabilities falling for two consecutive quarters would raise the bear-case weight.
4. MATCH Act passage including servicing would take about a fifth of revenue out of every case.
5. 2030 targets above €90bn at the 10 June 2027 Capital Markets Day would support the bull path.
